title: Language Arts 6
description: Grade 6 reading, writing, language, research, and speaking. Study a complete novel and original stories, informational texts, poems, and drama; build a portfolio of evidence-based, revised writing.
author: Erudior
changelog: Initial release: nine modules with 36 lessons, mixed-format quizzes, a complete novel and original reader texts, 36 writing workshops, nine rubrics, study cards, and reference sheets.

lessons.title: Evidence and quotations
lessons.body:
## Read with a question in mind

A strong reader notices details and explains why they matter. This course begins with a small story. You will return to its characters while practicing different reading methods. All modern stories, people, data, and organizations in this course's practice packets are fictional unless a source note says otherwise. Keep a reading notebook on paper or in your writing assignments. Record the title, a location, a detail, and your thinking. You do not need to underline every sentence.

## Read: The Last Shelf, part 1

> [1] On Friday, Mara arrived at the library with a cardboard model of a bridge. The model fit inside a shoebox, except for one crooked tower. She had promised to show it at the neighborhood exhibition. At the door she slowed, trying to hide the tower with her sleeve.
>
> [2] Inside, Tomas was arranging photographs on the last empty shelf. “I thought you weren't coming,” he said. Mara set the box behind a stack of books. “I had to finish something.” She pulled a strip of tape from her pocket and pressed it against the tower.
>
> [3] A younger child stopped beside her. “How does it stay up?” he asked. Mara began explaining the triangles beneath the road. Her hand moved away from the tower. When the librarian called for exhibitors, Mara carried the box to the table instead of leaving it behind the books.

## Say exactly what the text supports

**[[Textual evidence]]** is a detail from a text used to support an idea about it. A detail is not evidence for every possible claim. Mara carries a shoebox: that supports a statement about the model's size, not a statement about whether she dislikes Tomas. First identify the question, then choose a detail that answers it.

An **[[explicit detail]]** is directly stated. The story explicitly identifies Friday and a crooked tower. The story does not explicitly tell us Mara's age or what grade she receives. Distinguishing stated facts from your conclusions prevents an attractive guess from becoming an invented fact.

A **[[quotation]]** repeats a source's exact words. Put quotation marks around the words you copy. A **[[location reference]]** helps another reader find the evidence. Here, use paragraph numbers; in the novel, use chapter numbers because page numbers vary across editions. A reference does not replace an explanation. After citing, say how the detail supports the answer.

### Example 1: Choose relevant evidence

Question: What shows that Mara tries to hide a flaw? Step one: identify the idea to support—hiding a flaw, not arriving late. Step two: locate “trying to hide the tower with her sleeve” in paragraph 1. Step three: connect action to idea: the sleeve covers the crooked tower. A response can say, “Mara tries to conceal the model's flaw: she is ‘trying to hide the tower with her sleeve’ (paragraph 1).” Quoting the entire paragraph would bury the useful detail.

### Example 2: Repair an unsupported statement

Draft: “Mara is the youngest exhibitor, and everyone laughs at her.” Step one: look for the age comparison and laughter. Neither appears. Step two: replace the invented claim with a supported one: “Mara decides to exhibit her model.” Step three: support it with paragraph 3, where she carries the box to the table. The revision is less dramatic but more trustworthy. Analysis grows from what the text provides.

## Try it with a check

Which detail best supports “Mara knows something about how bridges work”: the Friday arrival, the hidden box, or her explanation of the triangles? Choose before reading on. The explanation is relevant because it shows her describing the model's structure. It does not prove that she knows everything about engineering. Good readers match the size of the conclusion to the size of the evidence.

Now copy a short quotation showing that Mara repairs the tower. Check it against paragraph 2 word by word. Include “paragraph 2” in your note. A quotation should not silently change a speaker or remove a word such as *not*, which could reverse its meaning. If you want different wording, paraphrase honestly instead of placing your wording inside quotation marks.

## Common mistakes

Avoid choosing a sentence merely because it contains the character's name. Avoid copying a quotation and stopping: your reader needs the connection. Avoid treating a correct location reference as proof that your interpretation is correct. Someone can cite the right paragraph and still draw an unsupported conclusion.

## Key points

- Read the question before selecting evidence.
- Separate stated details from conclusions.
- Quote accurately, identify a location, and explain the connection.
- Leave unknown information unknown.

## Revision clinic: choose the evidence that does the work

Imagine a response that says, “Mara wants to hide a flaw because she arrives on Friday.” The day is an explicit detail, but it does not explain concealment. Replace it with her action of covering the crooked tower. Now the evidence connects to the claim. A detail can be accurate and still be weak evidence for a particular interpretation.

Make a two-column note headed “My claim” and “What this detail supports.” Put the same claim beside two possible details. Explain the connection for each without adding an event that the passage never gives. Choose the stronger detail and explain why the other is less useful. This comparison helps you avoid selecting a quotation merely because it is easy to find.

Finally, compare the quoted words with the original. Keep the wording and punctuation accurate; if you quote only a phrase, make the surrounding sentence grammatical. Do not use quotation marks around a paraphrase. A reader should be able to tell which words belong to the source and which belong to your explanation. Before submitting, point to the exact phrase that supports your claim and say what reasoning connects them.

## Your writing workshop

Write a 120–220 word response explaining how Mara moves from hiding the model to presenting it. Use two details from different paragraphs of The Last Shelf, part 1. Quote one short phrase accurately and paraphrase the other detail. Identify both paragraph numbers. Do not invent an age, a grade, or an audience reaction.

Open the assignment below to save your work and use the rubric. You can also draft on paper, then type or paste it into the assignment. A quiz score checks the lesson’s bounded skills; it does not grade the quality of this writing.

```assignment
writing: la6-work-01
```

lessons.title: Making supported inferences
lessons.body:
## Go beyond a detail without leaving it behind

Readers often understand more than a narrator states directly. If someone checks a clock repeatedly and keeps a packed bag beside the door, you may infer that the person is waiting to leave. The text has not said so, and another explanation may be possible. An **[[inference]]** is a conclusion supported by textual clues and reasonable thinking. It is neither a direct quotation nor an unlimited guess.

## Read: The Last Shelf, part 2

> [1] At the exhibition table, Mara reached for the label reading “Perfect Bridge.” She folded it and put it in her pocket. On a blank card she wrote, “A Bridge That Is Still Being Built.”
>
> [2] Tomas examined the crooked tower. “Mine fell twice before I got it here,” he said, nodding toward a photograph of his paper arch. Mara laughed and loosened her grip on the box. “Then you know about tape.”
>
> [3] At closing time, the librarian asked whether Mara wanted to leave the model for the next day's visitors. Mara glanced at the tower. “Leave the tape beside it,” she said. “Someone might have a better idea.”

## Build and test an inference

A **[[clue]]** is a detail that helps you reach a conclusion. Here, Mara changes the label, laughs after hearing about Tomas's mistakes, and invites other people's ideas. These clues together suggest growing comfort with imperfect work. The final invitation supports this conclusion more strongly than the simple fact that she owns tape.

Use a three-part notebook entry: clue, possible inference, and explanation. Then look for **[[counterevidence]]**, a detail that would challenge your conclusion. If Mara had angrily ordered everyone away, the claim that she welcomed help would need revision. Good readers do not hide details that make an interpretation less convenient.

The **[[strength of support]]** is how closely and consistently the available evidence fits a conclusion. Use language such as *suggests*, *likely*, or *may* when the text leaves room for alternatives. These words do not excuse a weak guess. You still need a reason. “Mara may own a purple bicycle” remains unsupported because no bicycle clue appears.

### Example 1: Infer a change in attitude

Step one: collect a beginning clue—Mara removes “Perfect Bridge.” Step two: collect an ending clue—she invites a better idea. Step three: explain the relationship. The new title accepts unfinished work, and the invitation treats other people's ideas as useful. A supported inference is that Mara becomes more willing to share work that is not perfect. Avoid “Mara will never feel embarrassed again”; three paragraphs cannot establish a lifelong result.

### Example 2: Compare two possible explanations

Suppose a reader claims Mara laughs because she is mocking Tomas. Another claims she laughs because their shared difficulty makes her feel less alone. Compare the nearby dialogue: “Mine fell twice” is followed by “Then you know about tape,” and she loosens her grip. Those details better support connection and relief. The first explanation is possible in some other story, but this passage gives it less support. Reading is not a contest to produce the most surprising theory.

## Guided practice: a second setting

Read this original micro-scene: “Niko checked the address on the envelope, carried it to the blue house, and stopped with one hand above the bell. After a minute, he smoothed the envelope and knocked.” What can you infer? Hesitation before delivering the envelope is supported. The reason—an apology, an application, or a surprise—is unknown. A careful answer separates the supported hesitation from an invented explanation for it.

Write one inference and two details that support it. Then write a fact you cannot yet know. This final step trains you to notice the boundary of the evidence. If a later paragraph explains the letter, update your understanding. Changing an inference in response to new evidence is good reading, not failure.

## Common mistakes

Do not call every inference a fact. Do not rely only on what you personally would feel: different people can react differently. Do not use a stereotype about a group as evidence about a character. Study the individual's words and actions in this text. Finally, distinguish an inference about what has happened from a prediction about what might happen next.

## Key points

- Combine relevant clues with an explanation.
- Test an interpretation against nearby details and counterevidence.
- Use certainty that matches the support.
- Revise your inference when new information arrives.

## Revision clinic: calibrate an inference

Consider three statements: “Mara changes the sign,” “Mara may now be more willing to show unfinished work,” and “Mara will never feel embarrassed again.” The first reports an action. The second interprets the action in the context of her earlier behavior. The third predicts a permanent future state that the passage does not establish. Recognizing these different levels helps you choose wording that fits the evidence.

Use a confidence ladder in your notes: directly stated, strongly suggested, possible but uncertain, and unsupported. Place each of your draft's claims on the ladder. This is not a numerical probability calculation. It is a way to inspect the relationship between a claim and the text. A supported interpretation can still leave room for uncertainty.

Revise one statement by narrowing it rather than deleting the entire idea. For example, replace a prediction about all future exhibitions with a statement about this particular moment. Then find another detail that strengthens or complicates the inference. Explain what additional action would be needed to support a stronger claim. This exercise builds a habit of making interpretations neither timid nor more certain than their evidence allows.

## Your writing workshop

Explain one change you infer in Mara’s attitude in The Last Shelf, part 2. Use at least two clues and explain their connection. Then give one alternative interpretation and explain why it has less support. End with one question the story leaves unanswered.

Open the assignment below to save your work and use the rubric. You can also draft on paper, then type or paste it into the assignment. A quiz score checks the lesson’s bounded skills; it does not grade the quality of this writing.

```assignment
writing: la6-work-02
```

lessons.title: Summarizing without judging
lessons.body:
## Keep the important events and the author's meaning

A **[[summary]]** briefly presents a text's main ideas or important events in your own words. It is shorter than the original because it leaves out details that do not explain the central situation. It should still preserve what happened, why it mattered to the sequence, and how the situation changed. Summaries help you prepare for discussion, compare sources, and check your own understanding.

An **[[objective summary]]** separates the source's content from your personal judgment. You may enjoy or dislike a story, but “This boring story has a foolish main character” is an evaluation, not a summary. You can summarize a character making a mistake without insulting the character or praising the author.

## Read: The Repair Table

> [1] The library's exhibition was supposed to end on Saturday. Several visitors asked how the models had been made, and the librarian proposed a repair table for Sunday. Mara wanted to help, but she had promised to finish a poster with her cousin.
>
> [2] Mara suggested that Tomas run the first hour while she finished the poster. He agreed if she would label the supplies beforehand. They wrote a short list: tape for paper, string for hanging, and blank cards for questions. They left the tools that required an adult with the librarian.
>
> [3] On Sunday, the first visitor used a card to ask why a paper arch kept falling. Tomas read the question aloud. Three visitors offered different ideas. When Mara arrived with the finished poster, she added a drawing of the arch to it. The poster became a record of the group's questions instead of an advertisement for a perfect exhibition.

## Select, connect, and compress

A **[[major event]]** changes the main situation or explains an important decision. The request for a repair table, Mara's scheduling problem, the division of work, and the poster's new purpose are major events here. The exact colors of the cards, if the author had given them, would probably be minor details.

**[[Sequence]]** is the order of events. But a useful summary is not just a list beginning *then, then, then*. Show connections: *because*, *so*, *while*, or *after* can explain how a decision follows a problem. Do not add a cause the text never provides. If two events occur together, that alone does not establish that one caused the other.

### Example 1: Build a short summary

Step one: name the central situation—visitors want to learn how models work. Step two: name the obstacle—Mara has an earlier commitment. Step three: preserve the response—she and Tomas divide the work. Step four: include the meaningful outcome—the exhibition becomes a place for shared questions. Model: “When visitors ask for help with their models, the library adds a repair table. Mara and Tomas divide the work around Mara's earlier commitment. Visitors share ideas, and Mara turns her poster into a record of their questions.” This summary does not need every supply.

### Example 2: Remove judgment without losing meaning

Draft: “Mara selfishly abandons the brilliant Tomas, but she finally makes an amazing poster.” Step one: underline judgments—*selfishly*, *brilliant*, *amazing*. Step two: check events: Mara honors an earlier promise and arranges coverage rather than abandoning the table. Step three: replace judgment and distortion: “Mara finishes a promised poster while Tomas leads the first hour, then uses the poster to record the visitors' questions.” Objective does not mean vague; it means faithful to the source.

## Guided practice

Choose the more useful summary detail: “They use tape, string, and cards” or “They divide preparation and leading responsibilities.” For a brief summary of the whole story, the division of work matters more. If the task were to summarize the supply procedure, the supply list would become relevant. The purpose of a summary changes which details are central.

Write a one-sentence summary of paragraph 2. Possible response: “Mara and Tomas agree on a schedule and prepare clearly labeled supplies.” Check that the sentence retains the plan without claiming that the repair table has already happened. Summaries still need accurate time relationships.

## Common mistakes

Avoid retelling every action at the original length. Avoid shrinking so far that the result could describe any story: “People do things and learn.” Do not add your opinion as though it belongs to the source. Finally, do not mix up the author's message with a character's belief. A summary can report a belief without endorsing it.

## Key points

- Preserve the main situation, important response, and outcome.
- Select details according to the summary's purpose.
- Connect events accurately and use your own wording.
- Keep personal evaluation outside an objective summary.

## Revision clinic: keep the summary proportional

A draft summary might spend four sentences describing the repair-table supplies and only one sentence explaining how visitors' questions changed the poster. Count how much space each part receives, then compare that emphasis with the passage's main development. A summary should give central developments room to matter; it should not become a catalog of every object that appeared.

Try a three-stage note: situation, important development, outcome. Write one sentence for each stage, then combine or adjust them if the result feels mechanical. Keep necessary relationships clear. If removing a detail makes the sequence impossible to follow, it may deserve to stay. If removing it leaves the central development unchanged, it may be a detail to omit.

Check for judgment words such as foolish, wonderful, boring, or obviously. They may belong in an evaluated response, but an objective summary should describe the text without importing your approval. Also remove predictions about what happens after the passage ends. Read your summary to someone unfamiliar with the story, or imagine that reader yourself: can the person understand the main change without needing the original's minor details?

## Your writing workshop

Write a 100–160 word objective summary of The Repair Table. Then add a separate 40–70 word reflection explaining two details you left out and why. Clearly label Summary and Reflection so your selection choices are not confused with events in the story.

Open the assignment below to save your work and use the rubric. You can also draft on paper, then type or paste it into the assignment. A quiz score checks the lesson’s bounded skills; it does not grade the quality of this writing.

```assignment
writing: la6-work-03
```

lessons.title: Vocabulary in context
lessons.body:
## Make an informed word choice

An unfamiliar word is a problem you can investigate. **[[Context]]** is the surrounding language and situation that help establish meaning. Read the whole sentence, then the nearby sentences. A clue may define the word, offer an example, contrast it with another idea, or show how someone responds to it. One nearby word is not always enough.

Consider: “The committee's first plan was tentative: members expected to revise it after visitors tried the repair table.” The part after the colon explains that the plan may change. *Tentative* here means not final or firmly settled. It does not mean impossible, careless, or already successful. The context narrows the possibilities.

## Use word parts, then verify

A **[[prefix]]** is a meaningful part added at the beginning of a base, and a **[[suffix]]** is added at the end. In *reread*, *re-* means again. In *careless*, *-less* means without. Word parts provide clues, not automatic definitions for every word that looks similar. *Uncle* does not mean “not cle.” Check whether the proposed parts are real parts of that word.

A **[[reference entry]]** supplies information such as a word's meanings, pronunciation, grammatical role, and examples. A dictionary may list several meanings. Choose the one that fits the text. In “a draft of the poster,” *draft* means an early version, not moving air. If you choose the wrong sense, even a real dictionary definition will mislead you.

### Example 1: Infer and verify a word

Sentence: “Mara was reluctant to remove the first label; she held it for a moment before putting it away.” Step one: identify the action—she delays before removing the label. Step two: propose a meaning—unwilling or hesitant. Step three: substitute: “Mara was hesitant to remove the first label.” The sentence still makes sense. Step four: check a reference if available. Do not substitute “eager,” because it conflicts with the delay. Record both a short definition and the sentence that supported it.

### Example 2: Distinguish close meanings

Sentence: “Tomas gave a precise description: the arch used six paper strips, each folded twice.” Step one: notice that the example gives exact details. Step two: compare *precise* with *long*. A long description can still be unclear; this example emphasizes accuracy and specificity. Step three: use *exact* or *carefully specific* as the likely meaning. Step four: use the word in a new sentence: “The label gives precise directions for attaching the string.” This checks whether you can transfer the meaning to a new context.

## A small reference table

| Word in this lesson | Useful clue | Meaning in the example |
|---|---|---|
| tentative | expected to revise | not final |
| reluctant | delayed before acting | hesitant or unwilling |
| precise | six strips, folded twice | exact and carefully specific |
| draft | early poster version | a version prepared for revision |

The table is a learning aid, not a claim that each word has only one meaning. *Draft* can also name a current of air. Words move among contexts, so record the meaning you actually need.

## Guided practice

Read: “Unlike the rigid display board, the flexible strip bent around the model.” The contrast helps you infer that *flexible* means able to bend. Now test an alternative: “Unlike the rigid board, the colorful strip bent.” Color does not explain the contrast. Notice how the sentence's logic helps select a meaning, not merely any familiar adjective.

Try *reusable*. Identify *re-* as again, *use* as the base, and *-able* as able to be. Propose “able to be used again,” then check a sentence: “The reusable label can be erased and used at the next exhibition.” This case works; do not assume every unfamiliar word will break neatly into known pieces.

## Common mistakes

Do not stop reading at an unfamiliar word and guess from its first letter. Do not copy a dictionary's first meaning without checking the sentence. Avoid circular definitions such as “precision means being precise” when neither word is understood. When context is insufficient, mark the word for a reference check rather than pretending certainty.

## Key points

- Use nearby definitions, examples, contrasts, and actions.
- Treat word parts as clues to check.
- Select the reference meaning that fits the passage.
- Test a meaning by substituting it and using it in a new sentence.

## Revision clinic: combine clues instead of guessing once

When a word has several possible meanings, the first familiar definition may not fit. In a sentence about revising a draft, the surrounding verbs suggest a piece of writing rather than a current of air. In a sentence about a cold draft near a window, the setting points elsewhere. The letters alone do not settle the meaning; the word's job and the nearby ideas work together.

For an unfamiliar word, write a tentative meaning, underline the contextual clue, and test a replacement. Next, identify its grammatical job. Is it naming something, describing something, or showing an action? A replacement that changes that job may require a different form even if its general idea is close.

If context does not provide enough information, consult a dictionary or ask a knowledgeable reader. Compare the available meanings instead of copying the first entry. Record the meaning that fits this passage and an original sentence using it in a similar way. Revisit the word later in a different context. Knowing a word includes recognizing how its meaning can shift, not memorizing one substitution that must fit every appearance.

## Your writing workshop

Create four vocabulary notebook entries for tentative, reluctant, precise, and draft as used in this lesson. For each, give the meaning in context, identify a clue, and write a new sentence showing that meaning. Finish by explaining why a dictionary’s first definition might not fit every sentence.

Open the assignment below to save your work and use the rubric. You can also draft on paper, then type or paste it into the assignment. A quiz score checks the lesson’s bounded skills; it does not grade the quality of this writing.

```assignment
writing: la6-work-04
```

lessons.title: Plot, setting, and conflict
lessons.body:
## Begin a whole-book investigation

Open **The Wonderful Wizard of Oz** by L. Frank Baum in the Reading tab. This course includes all 24 chapters of the 1900 novel, not the later film. Read chapters 1–6 before completing this workshop. Divide the reading across several sessions; two chapters per session is a starting suggestion, not a speed requirement. The lesson's time estimate does not include every reading and writing session. Keep a chapter log with an important event, a character's goal, and one question.

This is a historical fantasy. Its magical events, including the house's flight, are not explanations of real weather. Its narrator sometimes uses old vocabulary and judgments about appearances. Identify those choices as part of the text rather than adopting them as descriptions of real people. The book includes threats, deaths, and fantastical injury; a parent or teacher can preview passages and support discussion.

## Track a goal through obstacles

**[[Setting]]** is a story's time and place, including conditions that shape what characters can do. **[[Plot]]** is the organized sequence of events and their connections. A **[[conflict]]** is a struggle involving incompatible goals, obstacles, or pressures. **[[Motivation]]** is what drives a character's action. These ideas work together: a cyclone changes Dorothy's setting and creates an obstacle to her desire to return home.

Do not confuse plot with a list of chapter titles. Ask what changes because of an event. Dorothy's house carries her away; she seeks a way home; advice sends her toward the Emerald City. Along the road, companions join because each hopes Oz will supply something they think they lack. Their separate goals create a shared journey.

### Example 1: Explain setting's effect

Step one: compare the gray Kansas surroundings in chapter 1 with the colorful country in chapter 2. Step two: identify the practical change: Dorothy is far from her family and does not know the route home. Step three: connect setting to action: the unfamiliar place makes seeking guidance necessary. “Oz is colorful” describes a feature. “The unfamiliar setting leads Dorothy to ask how to return to Kansas” explains an effect. Both can be true, but they answer different questions.

### Example 2: Trace motivation

In chapter 3, Dorothy frees the Scarecrow from a pole. He says he wants brains. Step one: record the stated goal without deciding yet whether he lacks intelligence. Step two: identify his choice to travel with Dorothy. Step three: explain the connection: the promise of help from Oz gives him a reason to join. A reader can distinguish what a character believes about himself from what his later actions demonstrate.

## A chapter log that shows connections

| Event | Immediate change | Question to keep reading for |
|---|---|---|
| Dorothy arrives in Oz | She must find a way home | Who can offer useful help? |
| The Scarecrow is freed | A companion joins the journey | Will his actions match his self-description? |
| Dorothy helps the Tin Woodman move again | Another traveler shares the route | What will he do when others need help? |

A log does not need to predict the correct ending. Its job is to preserve evidence and questions so that later chapters can change your understanding.

## Guided practice

The Lion describes himself as a coward in chapter 6. Does that statement alone prove that every action he takes will be cowardly? No. It is evidence of his self-perception. Record his stated goal and one action, then keep them separate in your notes. You will return to that comparison after reading more.

Choose one event from chapters 1–6 and complete: “Because ___ happened, ___ became possible or necessary.” Check the connection against the chapter. If you cannot explain it without inventing information, choose a different event or use a more limited claim. Stories can contain coincidence, so do not force every nearby event into a causal chain.

## Common mistakes

Do not substitute film details for the novel: in this text, Dorothy's shoes are silver. Do not label every inconvenience the main conflict. Do not assume the character's wish is the narrator's verdict about that character. Read the whole assigned section before judging which events matter most.

## Key points

- Track a goal, obstacle, choice, and consequence.
- Explain how setting shapes action.
- Separate self-description from demonstrated behavior.
- Cite the novel's chapters rather than an adaptation's scenes.

## Revision clinic: explain why an event matters

A plot log can become a list of disconnected events: Dorothy arrives, meets someone, travels, and faces a problem. To turn the list into analysis, add a relationship after each important event. What goal becomes clearer? What obstacle changes the available choices? What consequence makes the next event necessary or likely? These questions distinguish a connected plot from a calendar of happenings.

Choose one event from chapters 1–6 and write two sentences. The first reports the event accurately. The second explains its role in the developing conflict. Check that the second sentence does more than repeat the first using different words. If you claim an event caused a later choice, point to the connection in the chapter rather than assuming that every earlier event caused every later one.

Now imagine removing the event from your summary. If the main goal or an important relationship becomes hard to understand, explain that effect. You are not rewriting the published book; you are testing the event's function. Keep chapter numbers in your notes so you can return to the evidence when later chapters reveal a new consequence or change your interpretation.

## Your writing workshop

After reading chapters 1–6, create a six-entry chapter log and write a 180–280 word explanation of how Dorothy’s goal connects three important events. Include a setting detail and two chapter references. Add one question about a companion that later chapters could help answer.

Open the assignment below to save your work and use the rubric. You can also draft on paper, then type or paste it into the assignment. A quiz score checks the lesson’s bounded skills; it does not grade the quality of this writing.

```assignment
writing: la6-work-05
```

lessons.title: Character choices and change
lessons.body:
## Compare what characters say with what they do

Read chapters 7–12 of The Wonderful Wizard of Oz in the built-in reader. Continue your log, especially when someone helps another traveler. These chapters place the companions under pressure: they encounter a river, a dangerous poppy field, a city with an impressive ruler, and the Wicked Witch of the West. We analyze how characters respond, not how realistically the magic would work.

**[[Characterization]]** is the way a text develops a character through description, speech, thoughts, actions, and other characters' responses. A **[[trait]]** is a relatively lasting quality, while an **[[emotion]]** is a feeling in a particular moment. **[[Development]]** is a meaningful change or deepening of a character across a text. A frightened character can act bravely; a single anxious moment does not define every part of a person.

## Use more than a label

The Scarecrow wants brains, yet he offers useful ideas. The Tin Woodman wants a heart, yet he responds to others' needs. The Lion wants courage, yet he acts while afraid. These contrasts invite readers to question the companions' own descriptions. Do not jump from “acts kindly once” to “never acts unkindly.” Select several scenes and explain the pattern as far as it goes.

A character may remain recognizable while the reader's understanding develops. Sometimes the change is in what the character believes about himself; sometimes it is in what the reader notices. Name which kind of change you mean. “The Lion becomes brave” and “The reader recognizes courage in actions the Lion performs while afraid” are different claims and require different support.

### Example 1: Kindness before a reward

In chapter 9, the Tin Woodman saves a field mouse and says he tries to help those who need a friend. Step one: identify the action and explanation. Step two: compare them with his belief that he has no heart. Step three: reason about the contrast: his conduct already shows concern for another creature. The scene supports a discussion of kindness; it does not require a claim that a metal body has an ordinary human heart.

### Example 2: Ability and self-perception

The Scarecrow helps solve practical obstacles while describing himself as brainless. Step one: record a specific proposal from the journey. Step two: record his self-description. Step three: explain the gap. A response might argue that the story separates having confidence in an ability from using that ability. To strengthen the response, cite a second helpful action rather than merely repeating “He is smart” several times.

## Build a character evidence chart

| Self-description or wish | Action to examine | Possible interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| Wants a heart | Helps the mouse in chapter 9 | Concern may already be visible in behavior |
| Wants courage | Helps companions despite fear | Courage can involve action while afraid |
| Wants brains | Proposes ways around obstacles | Self-judgment can underestimate ability |

The interpretation column is not a list of universal truths proved by a fantasy. It records readings supported by this story. Another interpretation can be strong if it explains the details carefully.

## Guided practice

Read this original micro-scene: “Lena says she is impatient. She waits beside her brother while he ties his shoes, then asks him to teach her the knot.” Is patient behavior visible? Yes: she waits and shows interest. Does the scene prove she is always patient? No. Write an answer that includes both the useful evidence and its limit.

Return to the novel. Choose one moment when a companion's action and self-description differ. Use two columns before drafting: what the text says, and what you infer. This prevents a polished interpretation from hiding a missing detail. If you use a trait word such as considerate, explain the behavior that earns the label.

## Common mistakes

Avoid treating a character as one adjective. Avoid assuming every event changes the character permanently. Do not confuse your feelings about a character with the character's feelings. Above all, do not turn a nickname into unquestionable evidence: examine the narrative's actions and consequences.

## Key points

- Use speech, action, and response to study a character.
- Distinguish momentary emotion from a pattern of behavior.
- Compare self-perception with evidence.
- Explain whether the character changes or your understanding deepens.

## Revision clinic: test a character label

A character label such as brave, clever, or kind can be a useful starting hypothesis. It should not replace attention to actions. Make a note with four fields: situation, choice, consequence, and possible trait. A character who feels fear and still acts to help someone may complicate a simple definition of courage. Feeling and action are related, but they are not the same thing.

Choose two moments from the assigned chapters that bear on one trait. Describe what the character actually does before interpreting it. Ask whether the second moment confirms, complicates, or changes the first interpretation. Do not invent a motive merely because it would make the character consistent. Sometimes the most interesting analysis explains a tension between what a character says and what the character does.

Revise an absolute claim such as “This character is never afraid” into wording that accounts for the evidence. Then explain why the narrower claim is more informative, not merely safer. It can reveal how the character acts under a particular pressure. Keep the analysis grounded in this novel's chapter details, since an adaptation may change events or emphasize a different aspect of the character.

## Your writing workshop

After reading chapters 7–12, write a 220–350 word character analysis of one companion. Compare a stated wish or self-description with two specific actions. Explain whether the actions support or complicate that description. Include chapter references and one sentence limiting your conclusion.

lessons.title: Narrator and point of view
lessons.body:
## Ask who tells and who knows

Read chapters 13–18 of The Wonderful Wizard of Oz. The travelers return to the Emerald City, discover information about Oz, receive promised rewards, and face another problem in Dorothy's search for home. These developments change what characters and readers understand. Keep track of who knows a fact at each point; do not assume someone knew it before the story revealed it.

The **[[narrator]]** is the voice that tells a story. The author is the real person who created the text; the narrator is a storytelling role. **[[Point of view]]** is the position from which events are presented. A **[[first-person narrator]]** speaks as “I” or “we” within the story. A **[[third-person narrator]]** refers to characters as “he,” “she,” or “they.” Pronouns are a starting clue, not the whole analysis: you must also ask whose thoughts and knowledge the narration reveals.

## Track the range of knowledge

Third-person narration can stay near one character's experience or reveal several characters' thoughts. Baum's narrator can move among characters and tell readers information Dorothy does not yet know. In chapter 12, for example, the narration gives the Witch's thinking about Dorothy and the shoes. That access matters because readers can understand a danger or motive that Dorothy does not fully understand at the time.

An individual character's perspective is narrower than all the information a narrator may provide. Oz's claim to be a powerful wizard is something characters hear. Later revelations change how readers interpret the earlier performance. A narrator reporting a character's words does not guarantee that those words are accurate. Identify the source of each claim inside the story.

### Example 1: Separate speaker and narrator

Consider this original pair: “I will fix the arch,” Tomas said. Mara watched him search for tape. Step one: notice that “I” occurs inside Tomas's quotation. Step two: examine the storytelling outside it: “Tomas said” and “Mara watched.” Step three: conclude that the passage uses third-person narration with first-person dialogue. A quoted “I” does not turn the entire story into first person.

### Example 2: Change the viewpoint and examine the loss

Original: “Mara hid the label. Tomas thought she was hiding a prize.” Rewrite from Mara's first-person position: “I hid the label and saw Tomas watching me.” Step one: preserve what Mara can observe. Step two: remove direct access to Tomas's private thought unless he later tells her. Step three: explain the effect: readers know less about Tomas's misunderstanding. A viewpoint change is not just replacing names with pronouns; it changes available information.

## Compare knowledge at a turning point

| Moment | What characters may believe | What later evidence changes |
|---|---|---|
| Before Oz is exposed | His impressive appearances demonstrate power | The performance has a human explanation |
| After the discovery | Promises must be reconsidered | Companions still seek help and reassurance |
| Before the balloon departure | That plan might carry Dorothy home | Dorothy must seek another route |

Use chapter references when explaining these shifts. Avoid treating knowledge gained later as something a character obviously possessed earlier. Readers rereading a book have an advantage the characters do not share.

## Guided practice

Rewrite two sentences of The Last Shelf from Mara's first-person point of view. Keep observed actions, her own thoughts that you intentionally add, and details she can know. Label the result an adaptation; invented thoughts belong to your creative version, not to evidence about the original. Then name one detail you could no longer state with certainty.

## Common mistakes

Do not equate author and narrator. Do not identify the whole viewpoint from a single pronoun in dialogue. Avoid saying that every third-person narrator knows everything. Study what the actual passage reveals. When a character makes a questionable claim, attribute it to that character rather than silently reporting it as a fact.

## Key points

- Identify the telling voice and its access to knowledge.
- Distinguish narration from quoted dialogue.
- Track what is revealed and when.
- Explain how a viewpoint shapes what readers can understand.

## Revision clinic: track who knows what

Draw three columns in your notes: character knowledge, reader knowledge, and information still uncertain. Choose a moment from chapters 13–18 and fill the columns with details the text actually provides at that point. Avoid adding information from the end of the book to a character's earlier understanding. Knowing the ending can make it easy to forget what was uncertain during the journey.

Next, examine one sentence of your analysis. If it says “Dorothy knows,” locate the evidence that she has learned the information by that moment. If it says “The reader learns,” identify how the narrator presents it. If neither is supported, revise the sentence to identify an inference or a later discovery instead. This check makes discussions of surprise and suspense more precise.

As a stretch task, rewrite a short event from another character's limited viewpoint. Use only what that character could observe or reasonably infer. Then explain one fact your version must omit and one detail it might emphasize. Label the new passage as your adaptation, not a quotation from Baum. The comparison should show how perspective changes access to information even when the underlying event remains the same.

## Your writing workshop

After reading chapters 13–18, explain how a revelation about Oz changes the interpretation of an earlier scene. Use two chapter references. Then rewrite a short moment from Dorothy’s first-person viewpoint and label it Creative adaptation. Explain one piece of information that viewpoint cannot directly know.

lessons.title: Theme across a whole novel
lessons.body:
## Finish the novel before choosing its larger meaning

Read chapters 19–24 of The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, then revisit your notes from the beginning. You have now read the whole novel. The final chapters bring more obstacles, a meeting with Glinda, a way home, and a brief return to Aunt Em. A whole-book interpretation must account for that ending as well as the scenes you liked most.

A **[[theme]]** is a larger idea a literary work develops about experience. A **[[topic]]** is a subject such as friendship, courage, or home. A **[[theme statement]]** expresses an idea about a topic in a complete sentence. **[[Synthesis]]** brings evidence from different parts into a connected understanding. “Friendship” is a topic; “People can accomplish difficult goals by recognizing and combining different strengths” is a possible theme statement to test.

## A theme is developed, not merely announced

Do not hunt for one magical sentence that dictates every meaning. Compare choices, consequences, repeated contrasts, and the ending. The companions want qualities that their actions already suggest. Dorothy values returning home even after seeing wonders. Helpers with different strengths contribute at different moments. These patterns can support more than one defensible interpretation.

A good theme statement is broad enough to matter beyond one named character but specific enough to explain the text. “Things happen” says almost nothing. “Dorothy travels to Oz” summarizes plot. “A person's worth can be visible in helpful actions before that person recognizes it” proposes a larger meaning. It still needs evidence and careful limits; a novel does not prove that every person already has every needed skill.

### Example 1: Test a theme across the book

Proposed theme: different strengths make cooperation valuable. Step one: choose an early example of companions joining with different needs. Step two: choose a middle example in which their different abilities help the group, such as the cooperation around the river or the rescue involving the mice. Step three: explain how the examples connect. Step four: test the ending: companions reach different destinations rather than all wanting exactly the same future. The theme allows difference within friendship.

### Example 2: Revise an overbroad theme

Draft: “You never need help because you already have everything.” Step one: test it against Dorothy's dependence on guidance and her companions' help. The claim does not fit. Step two: preserve the useful insight about underestimating oneself. Step three: revise: “People may overlook strengths they already use, and others can help them recognize those strengths.” This version fits the contrast between abilities and self-perception without denying the importance of assistance.

## Compare without flattening differences

Return to the original Last Shelf story. Mara becomes more willing to share an imperfect model after conversation and a visitor's question. The novel's companions seek reassurance about qualities visible in their actions. A comparison can connect self-confidence while acknowledging that the plots, scale, and outcomes differ.

| Text | Evidence to examine | Possible shared idea |
|---|---|---|
| The Last Shelf | A revised label and an invitation for ideas | Others can help someone reconsider a self-judgment |
| The Wonderful Wizard of Oz | Wishes contrasted with helpful actions | Abilities may be visible before confidence catches up |

The table prepares an argument; it does not replace one. Explain the link and one difference. Avoid claiming that two stories have identical meanings merely because both include friends.

## Guided practice

Choose between “home” and “A valued home can matter more to a character than unfamiliar wonders.” The first is a topic; the second is a theme statement you could test using Dorothy's repeated goal and the ending. Find an early and a late chapter reference. If your evidence supports only a narrower claim, revise the statement instead of stretching the evidence.

## Common mistakes

Avoid moral commands that do not fit the plot. Do not treat a personal lesson as automatically the author's intended message. You can say “The pattern suggests” rather than claiming direct knowledge of the author's mind. Use the ending, but do not ignore conflicting details from earlier chapters.

## Key points

- Move from a topic to a complete, testable theme statement.
- Connect evidence from beginning, middle, and ending.
- Revise claims that ignore important counterexamples.
- Compare shared ideas and meaningful differences.

## Revision clinic: move from topic to theme

Write a topic word from the novel, then turn it into a complete statement about what the story suggests. Avoid statements so broad that almost any book would support them, such as “Things happen to people.” Also avoid treating a theme as a command every reader must obey. Literary analysis examines how the work develops an idea through its particular events and choices.

Create an evidence trail with an early moment, a middle moment, and a late moment. Explain the contribution of each. Three examples that repeat the same observation may be less useful than examples that reveal change, tension, or a qualification. Include a moment that initially seems to challenge your theme statement. Decide whether your interpretation can explain it or needs revision.

Finish by comparing your theme with a plausible alternative. Both may be defensible. Explain how your selected evidence makes your interpretation useful without claiming that every other reading is wrong. A strong final response accounts for the complete novel and distinguishes analysis from personal preference. You can dislike an event and still analyze its role accurately; you can enjoy a character and still discuss a difficult choice.

## Your writing workshop

Write a 350–500 word whole-novel analysis of one theme. Include evidence from at least three chapters, including an early and a late chapter. Explain how the pattern develops. Add a short comparison with The Last Shelf, identifying both a shared idea and a difference. End by revising one overbroad claim you considered.

lessons.title: Central ideas and supporting details
lessons.body:
## Find the idea the details build

Informational writing explains, describes, reports, or argues about a subject. Its **[[central idea]]** is the main point developed across a passage. A **[[supporting detail]]** helps explain, illustrate, or establish that point. A **[[topic sentence]]** states a paragraph's main idea, when the paragraph includes one explicitly. **[[Elaboration]]** adds explanation, examples, or connections that develop an idea. These tools help readers follow more than a list of facts.

## Read: A Place for Questions

This report and its numbers describe an invented library project. Treat them as evidence within the practice packet, not as findings about real libraries.

> [1] Brook Lane Library tested a repair table during four Sunday afternoons. Visitors brought paper models, loose book covers, and questions about craft projects. The librarian recorded 12, 18, 15, and 19 visits on the four days. A visit was counted when someone stopped at the table; the same person could count on more than one day.
>
> [2] At first, the table had only supplies and a sign reading “Ask here.” Some visitors waited without speaking. The volunteers then added question cards and a small example of a repaired paper arch. The cards let a visitor ask a question before deciding whether to speak to the group.
>
> [3] The cards also changed the volunteers' work. Instead of repeating instructions separately, they grouped similar questions and made one short demonstration. A volunteer wrote that the cards helped visitors see that other people were puzzled too. The report did not measure whether anyone's model lasted longer afterward.

## Test a central idea against all paragraphs

“The report is about a library” names the topic but not the point. “Question cards changed how visitors asked for help and how volunteers responded” captures the development across paragraphs 2 and 3. Paragraph 1 sets the context and defines the visit counts. A central idea does not need to mention every number, but it should explain why the major details belong together.

Do not confuse a memorable detail with the central idea. Nineteen visits on the last day is specific and easy to remember, but the passage develops the process of asking and grouping questions. Likewise, an exciting claim such as “The cards made all models stronger” goes beyond the report, which explicitly says durability was not measured.

### Example 1: Connect a detail to the central idea

Step one: choose the detail that cards let visitors ask before speaking publicly. Step two: ask what that illustrates: the cards provide another way to participate. Step three: connect it to the proposed central idea about changing how help is requested. The explanation should name the link, not merely repeat the detail. A good response says, “The cards changed participation by allowing a written question before a public conversation.”

### Example 2: Explain elaboration

Compare “The volunteers changed their method” with paragraph 3's account of grouping similar questions and demonstrating once. Step one: identify the broad statement. Step two: identify the concrete example. Step three: explain how the example develops the idea: it shows what changed and why the change reduced repeated explanation. Elaboration answers a reader's likely question: “What do you mean, and how does that work?”

## Use numbers with their definitions

The four daily counts total 64 visits, but that is not necessarily 64 different people. The report defines a visit, so an accurate summary preserves that unit. A central-idea paragraph may not need the sum at all. If you include it, explain its role and avoid converting a count into proof of satisfaction or learning. A number becomes useful evidence when you know what it measures.

## Guided practice

Which detail supports the idea that written questions can reveal shared confusion: the exact date of a Sunday or the volunteer's note that visitors saw others were puzzled too? The note directly supports the idea. Now distinguish observation from limitation: the report describes a change in the discussion process but does not measure lasting repair success. Both belong in a careful reading.

Write a two-sentence summary. Sentence one should state the main development; sentence two should include one strong detail or important limit. Keep your personal opinion about libraries separate from what this report says.

## Common mistakes

Do not treat the first sentence as automatically the central idea. Do not select a statement too broad to fit this particular passage. Avoid replacing the measured unit with a more impressive one. Details should develop the idea, not merely decorate your answer.

## Key points

- Distinguish a subject from a developed point.
- Test the central idea against multiple paragraphs.
- Explain how examples elaborate a broad statement.
- Preserve the meaning and limits of reported numbers.

## Revision clinic: distinguish topic, idea, and detail

Write three headings: topic, central idea, and supporting detail. Under topic, name the subject in a few words. Under central idea, state what the passage develops about that subject. Under supporting detail, record an example or observation that helps establish the idea. If all three entries say almost the same thing, reread and revise them until their different jobs are clear.

For A Place for Questions, a response that only says “a repair table” names a subject. A fuller statement should explain how the project created a place for asking and recording questions. The attendance figures may support a discussion of use, but they do not by themselves capture every idea about participation. Select details that fit the central idea you are explaining.

Check whether your statement is broad enough to cover the important paragraphs but narrow enough to fit this text. If it describes only the first paragraph, extend it. If it makes a claim about every library everywhere, narrow it. Then write a sentence explaining how one detail develops the idea. That final connection is what turns a selected fact into purposeful supporting evidence.

## Your writing workshop

Write a 180–280 word explanation of the central idea of A Place for Questions. Use a detail from paragraph 2 and another from paragraph 3. Explain how each develops the idea. Add one accurate sentence about what the visit counts do and do not establish.

lessons.title: How text structure develops ideas
lessons.body:
## Notice the relationship, not just the headings

**[[Text structure]]** is the way a writer organizes ideas and their relationships. A **[[chronological structure]]** follows time order. A **[[cause-and-effect structure]]** explains how or why one event contributes to another. A **[[problem-and-solution structure]]** identifies a difficulty and a response. Writers also compare alternatives, classify examples, or describe parts of a whole. One article can combine several structures.

Signal words can help, but they do not decide the answer alone. *Before* may signal time; *because* may signal cause; *instead* may signal contrast. Read the relationship the whole passage develops. A paragraph with the word *after* can still mainly explain a problem and its attempted solution.

## Read: Three ways to explain the same project

> A. On the first Sunday, volunteers placed supplies on the table. On the second, they added question cards. On the third, they grouped similar cards. On the fourth, they displayed the most common questions beside the examples.
>
> B. Some visitors waited without asking questions. To make participation easier, volunteers offered blank question cards. The cards allowed written questions and helped volunteers organize a shared demonstration. The report does not show whether the cards helped every visitor.
>
> C. The first sign gave only an invitation: “Ask here.” The revised sign included an invitation and an example question. Both signs welcomed visitors, but the example made the expected action more concrete.

All three excerpts are original fictional practice texts. They describe related information but direct attention differently. A highlights sequence, B highlights a difficulty and response, and C compares two versions. Structure is a decision about what readers should notice.

### Example 1: Explain the effect of time order

Step one: find the organizing pattern in A—first through fourth Sunday. Step two: identify the benefit: readers can follow how the project developed. Step three: identify the limit: a time-ordered list alone does not prove which change caused a later result. A useful analysis says, “The chronological structure makes the stages clear, but it does not establish that the cards caused the higher visit count.” This explains both what the structure does and what it cannot do.

### Example 2: Explain a paragraph's job

In B, the first sentence identifies waiting without asking. The next sentence introduces cards as a response. Step one: name the problem. Step two: locate the proposed solution. Step three: explain how the final limitation qualifies the response. If you remove the last sentence, readers may overestimate how thoroughly the method was tested. A sentence can be important because it limits a claim, not only because it adds a new fact.

## Plan a structure before drafting

| Your reader needs to understand | A useful structure | A question to check |
|---|---|---|
| How a project developed | Chronological | Are stages in a clear time order? |
| How two choices differ | Comparison | Are the same features compared? |
| How a difficulty was addressed | Problem and solution | Is the response connected to the actual problem? |
| Why an outcome occurred | Cause and effect | Is the claimed connection supported? |

The structure should fit the purpose. Do not force a comparison into a timeline simply because you know the dates. To compare two signs fairly, examine the same features—invitation, example, and clarity—rather than comparing one sign's color with the other sign's cost.

## Guided practice

Read: “The cards became wet when the table stood beside an open window. Because the ink blurred, volunteers moved the table and placed a cover over the cards.” What relationship is emphasized? The wet cards and blurred ink explain the response, so cause and effect is prominent within a problem-and-response account. More than one structural description can be reasonable if you explain the level you are discussing.

Now write two versions of a three-sentence explanation: one ordered by time and one organized around a problem. Keep the facts the same. Compare what each version makes easiest to understand. This experiment shows that organization changes emphasis without requiring new facts.

## Common mistakes

Do not assume one signal word labels an entire article. Avoid calling events causes merely because they occur earlier. Do not identify a structure and stop; explain how it helps readers understand the subject. When analyzing a sentence, describe its role in the surrounding paragraph.

## Key points

- Identify the relationship connecting ideas.
- Explain how structure serves the reader's purpose.
- Distinguish a sequence from a proven cause.
- Notice examples, transitions, and limiting sentences.

## Revision clinic: explain a structural choice

A writer may use sequence to show how a project unfolded and comparison to examine two ways of organizing it. These structures can coexist. Instead of forcing an entire text into one label, identify the passage or relationship you are discussing and explain what that organization helps readers understand. Signal words are useful clues, but the actual relationship among ideas matters more than one word.

Take a short portion of the project account and outline its present structure. Then try an alternative organization: for instance, group all access problems together and all responses together instead of reporting events in order. Keep the underlying facts unchanged. Compare what becomes easier and what becomes harder to follow. An organizational choice may highlight a connection while making chronology less visible.

In your explanation, name both the technique and its effect. “The writer uses sequence” identifies a structure. “The sequence lets readers see which adjustment followed the first session's problem” explains why it matters. Add a precise detail from the text so the analysis is checkable. The goal is not to declare one structure best for every purpose, but to choose and evaluate structure in relation to a reader's needs.

## Your writing workshop

Use the fictional repair-table facts to write two short explanations: one chronological and one organized as problem and solution. Then write a paragraph explaining how the structures change the emphasis. Preserve the same facts and include a limitation rather than claiming the method helped everyone.

lessons.title: Purpose, perspective, and claims
lessons.body:
## Read for what the writer wants you to think or do

An author's **[[purpose]]** is what the text is trying to accomplish: explain a process, persuade an audience, report results, entertain, or some combination. **[[Perspective]]** is the position or outlook shaping what a writer notices and emphasizes. A **[[claim]]** is a statement that can be supported or challenged. **[[Credibility]]** is the degree of trust a source deserves for the particular information you need. These are questions to investigate, not labels to apply from appearance alone.

## Read: Two messages about evening access

Both messages below concern the invented Brook Lane Library. The named writers are fictional, and the data are practice data.

> Message A — Student exhibition group: “Please test a Thursday evening exhibition hour. Of 30 visitors who voluntarily answered our paper survey at Saturday's exhibition, 18 said they would prefer an evening option. A four-week trial would let us count actual evening visits. We have not surveyed people who could not attend Saturday.”
>
> Message B — Building coordinator: “An evening trial needs a staffed entrance and a closing plan. The room is currently available on four Thursdays. I can confirm the room schedule, but I cannot promise that the trial would attract more visitors than Saturday. Please submit a staffing plan before a decision.”

## Identify evidence and limits

A's purpose is to persuade decision-makers to try evening access. B's purpose is to explain operational requirements. Their purposes differ, but that does not make one automatically honest and the other dishonest. A acknowledges a sampling limit. B distinguishes schedule knowledge from a prediction about attendance. These qualifications can make the messages more useful.

The survey describes the 30 volunteers who answered at one event. It does not establish what every resident wants. The coordinator has relevant access to room scheduling, but that role does not supply attendance data. Credibility depends partly on expertise, access to evidence, method, transparency, and fit to the question. A well-designed source can still have a limited scope.

### Example 1: Trace a specific claim

Claim: an evening trial is worth considering. Step one: locate the stated support—18 of 30 respondents preferred an evening option. Step two: explain the link: some current visitors expressed interest. Step three: name the limit: the voluntary Saturday survey excludes some potential visitors and does not measure actual evening attendance. The evidence can support a trial without proving it will succeed. A reasonable conclusion should preserve that difference.

### Example 2: Match a source to a question

Question: Is the room available on the proposed Thursdays? Step one: identify who has direct scheduling information—the coordinator. Step two: locate the precise confirmation—four Thursdays are available. Step three: avoid borrowing unrelated authority: this scheduling knowledge does not prove demand. If the question changes to what visitors prefer, the survey becomes relevant, although its limits remain.

## Notice perspective without attacking a person

The student group emphasizes access and interest. The coordinator emphasizes staffing and closure. Both can contribute to a decision. Instead of writing “The coordinator hates students,” describe the observable emphasis and support it with a phrase. Perspective analysis is about what the message foregrounds, not inventing a secret motive.

Words can signal a stronger claim than the evidence permits. Compare “Some surveyed visitors preferred evenings” with “Everyone demands evenings.” The second changes both the population and the certainty. Check pronouns and quantifiers such as *all*, *some*, *always*, and *never*. Small words can make large differences.

## Guided practice

Write a margin note for each message: purpose, strongest evidence, and unresolved question. For A, an unresolved question is actual trial attendance. For B, it might be who can staff the entrance. These are useful next questions because they arise from the sources' limits, not from unrelated curiosity.

## Common mistakes

Do not assume a professional title makes every claim reliable. Do not assume an interested writer cannot supply useful evidence. Avoid treating disagreement as proof of dishonesty. Most importantly, do not turn a small or selective sample into a statement about everyone.

## Key points

- Identify purpose and the evidence for it.
- Match source knowledge to the specific question.
- Distinguish a supported claim from a prediction.
- Explain perspective through emphasis, wording, and selection.

## Revision clinic: separate perspective from error

A student group and a building coordinator may emphasize different concerns because they have different responsibilities. That difference alone does not establish that one speaker is dishonest. Identify what each message wants readers to notice, then check its factual statements and reasoning independently. A source can have a clear perspective and still provide useful evidence.

Make a comparison note with the columns purpose, selected evidence, concern, and unanswered question. Fill each column for both evening-access messages. Keep observations separate from guesses about private motives. If you infer that a writer values dependable staffing, connect that inference to the stated conditions rather than inventing a personal history.

Now revise a sentence such as “The coordinator hates evening access” if the message only says staffing and closing plans are needed. A more accurate statement identifies the condition and leaves the private feeling unknown. Ask how the two messages could inform a shared decision: interest helps explain why a trial might be useful, while operational constraints help define how it could run. Analyzing purpose should make the disagreement clearer without turning different priorities into unsupported accusations.

## Your writing workshop

Compare Messages A and B in 220–320 words. Identify each purpose and area of relevant knowledge. Explain what the survey supports and what it cannot establish. Recommend one additional piece of information a decision-maker should seek before approving a trial.

lessons.title: Comparing texts and media
lessons.body:
## Compare evidence across formats

A written report, a chart, a photograph, and a spoken explanation can address the same topic while contributing different information. **[[Medium]]** is the form used to communicate. **[[Representation]]** is the particular way information is shown or described. **[[Corroboration]]** occurs when sources provide supporting evidence for the same claim. A **[[discrepancy]]** is a difference that needs explanation. Agreement is useful, but two copies of the same unsupported statement are not independent proof.

## Read: A report, a table, and a caption

The following fictional materials concern the same four repair-table Sundays.

> Report: “The repair table recorded 12 visits in week 1, 18 in week 2, 15 in week 3, and 19 in week 4. Volunteers counted visits, not unique individuals. The count went down in week 3 and rose in week 4.”

| Week | Counted visits |
|---|---:|
| 1 | 12 |
| 2 | 18 |
| 3 | 15 |
| 4 | 19 |

> Proposed poster caption: “Every week brings more people than the week before!”

The report and table agree on the numbers. The caption does not: week 3 is lower than week 2. The last value is higher than the first, but that is different from increasing every week. A strong comparison names the exact agreement or disagreement instead of saying the sources are simply “similar.”

## Ask what each form contributes

The table makes exact values easy to locate. The report defines the unit and describes the pattern. A line chart could make the rise, dip, and rise visible, but it would still need labeled axes and a clear scale. A photograph might show the table arrangement or a moment of participation; one photograph cannot establish total attendance for all four days.

Pictures and numbers do not explain themselves. Ask when a picture was taken, what lies outside its frame, and whether a caption accurately describes it. Ask what a number counts and whether the display includes all relevant categories. The purpose is careful interpretation, not automatic distrust of every visual.

### Example 1: Repair a misleading caption

Step one: identify the caption's claim—each week exceeds the previous one. Step two: compare each adjacent pair: 12 to 18 rises, 18 to 15 falls, and 15 to 19 rises. Step three: revise to a supported statement: “Visits were higher in week 4 than week 1, with a dip in week 3.” Step four: preserve the unit *visits*. Replacing it with *new members* would create a new unsupported claim.

### Example 2: Explain complementary information

Question: Does the table tell us whether 64 different people attended? Step one: add the values if the total is useful: 64 visits. Step two: read the report's definition: repeated visitors can be counted on different days. Step three: combine the forms: “The table gives 64 visits in total; the report explains that this is not a count of unique people.” The explanation uses both sources rather than letting the more visual one overrule the written qualification.

## Compare accounts of an event

Suppose a volunteer's note says the question cards were useful, while a visitor's note says the supplies were hard to find. These comments need not contradict each other. They describe different aspects of one experience. A synthesis could say the question system helped one process while the supply layout still needed improvement. Before declaring a conflict, check whether the sources answer the same question, use the same time period, and mean the same thing by their terms.

## Guided practice

Write a caption for the table in no more than two sentences. Include the main pattern and one limit. Then explain what a photograph could add: perhaps the placement of signs or the grouping of visitors. State what it could not add by itself: the full four-week attendance total or every participant's opinion.

## Common mistakes

Do not equate a larger final value with uninterrupted growth. Do not compare unlike units, such as visits and different people. Do not treat an image's vividness as evidence of typicality. Check whether supposedly independent reports share the same original source.

## Key points

- Compare exact claims, units, dates, and definitions.
- Explain what each medium contributes.
- Resolve apparent contradictions by checking scope.
- Revise captions to match the actual evidence.

## Revision clinic: inspect a caption independently

A caption is another claim to evaluate, even when it appears directly beneath a trustworthy table. Cover the caption and describe the numerical pattern yourself. Then uncover it and compare each part of its wording with the values. This simple separation can reveal when a persuasive sentence goes beyond the data it accompanies.

Use the Sunday figures to write two accurate captions with different emphases. One might emphasize the total use; another might note that the last count is higher than the first despite an intermediate decrease. Both can be accurate if their wording preserves the units and period. An accurate caption need not mention every possible observation, but it must not imply a pattern the table contradicts.

Next, imagine a reader who cannot see the table. Write a short description that gives the needed values and explains the relevant pattern. Avoid relying on color, position, or “the large one.” Compare the description with the surrounding report: does the report explain something the table alone cannot, such as why questions were recorded? Explain how the two forms can complement each other while still requiring separate checks for accuracy and overstatement.

## Your writing workshop

Create an accurate two-sentence caption for the four-week table, then write a 180–260 word comparison of the report, table, and misleading proposed caption. Explain one agreement, one discrepancy, and one question that none of the materials can answer.
