Put your new wording in exact quotation marks.
Change the speaker and call it a quotation.
Add a missing event to make it clearer.
questions.explanation: A paraphrase uses your wording while preserving and crediting the source’s meaning.

questions.stem: Which actions help a reader use evidence responsibly? Select all that apply.
choices: Check copied words against the passage.
Invent a missing event.
Explain how a detail supports the claim.
Choose any line containing the character’s name.
questions.explanation: Accurate copying and a clear connection make the evidence checkable and relevant.

questions.stem: What term names the exact borrowed words of a source: quotation or prediction?
questions.explanation: A quotation repeats the source’s exact words.

questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning in this lesson.
choices: A detail from a text used to support an idea about it
Information directly stated in the text
The exact words of a source, marked as borrowed words
Information that helps a reader find a detail in a source
questions.explanation: textual evidence: A detail from a text used to support an idea about it; explicit detail: Information directly stated in the text; quotation: The exact words of a source, marked as borrowed words; location reference: Information that helps a reader find a detail in a source.

questions.stem: Niko pauses before knocking and smooths an envelope twice. Which inference has the best support?
choices: He wants to buy the house.
He is delivering a birthday card.
He hesitates before delivering it.
He has already won a contest.
questions.explanation: The hesitation is observable through the pause and repeated action; the envelope’s purpose is not given.

questions.stem: Mara replaces “Perfect Bridge” with “A Bridge That Is Still Being Built.” What does the new label suggest?
choices: She has destroyed the model.
She plans to forbid visitors.
She thinks all bridges are perfect.
She is more willing to acknowledge unfinished work.
questions.explanation: The replacement title openly accepts that work can remain unfinished.

questions.stem: Which response correctly separates evidence from inference?
choices: She loosens her grip; this may suggest relief.
She feels relief because the narrator directly names it.
She always loves exhibitions because she owns tape.
She is relieved, so every future project will succeed.
questions.explanation: Loosening her grip is stated; relief is a supported interpretation rather than a named fact.

questions.stem: A reader says Mara welcomes advice. Which added detail would most challenge that claim?
choices: She listens to Tomas’s experience.
She tells every visitor to keep suggestions to themselves.
She asks a visitor for a better idea.
She leaves tape beside the model.
questions.explanation: Refusing suggestions would challenge the claim of welcoming advice.

questions.stem: Why is “Mara may own a purple bicycle” still unsupported?
choices: An inference must quote every paragraph.
A character cannot own a bicycle.
No relevant bicycle clue appears.
The word may always makes a claim false.
questions.explanation: Cautious wording cannot replace relevant evidence.

questions.stem: Which conclusion overstates the passage’s support?
choices: Mara changes the model’s label.
Mara invites ideas for the model.
Mara laughs during the conversation.
Mara will never feel embarrassed again.
questions.explanation: The passage shows a local change, not a guarantee about all future feelings.

questions.stem: Two interpretations conflict. What is the best next step?
choices: Compare how well each fits the text’s details.
Choose the one that sounds most surprising.
Ignore details that disagree with your first idea.
Treat both as equally supported automatically.
questions.explanation: Interpretations can have different levels of support; compare them against the evidence.

questions.stem: A later paragraph reveals why Niko brought the envelope. What should a reader do?
choices: Pretend the information appeared earlier.
Update earlier inferences using the new information.
Reject it if it disagrees with an earlier guess.
Keep every first impression unchanged.
questions.explanation: Reading is cumulative; new evidence can confirm or change a conclusion.

questions.stem: Which statements model careful inference? Select all that apply.
choices: Owning tape proves she is always confident.
The repeated clock checks suggest impatience.
Every possible interpretation has equal support.
The reason for the hesitation is not yet stated.
questions.explanation: Careful readers connect clues to limited conclusions and identify what remains unknown.

questions.stem: What term means a conclusion supported by clues: inference or quotation?
questions.explanation: An inference goes beyond a stated detail while remaining supported by it.

questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning in this lesson.
choices: A conclusion supported by clues and reasonable thinking
A detail that helps a reader reach a conclusion
A detail that challenges a proposed conclusion
How closely and consistently evidence fits a conclusion
questions.explanation: inference: A conclusion supported by clues and reasonable thinking; clue: A detail that helps a reader reach a conclusion; counterevidence: A detail that challenges a proposed conclusion; strength of support: How closely and consistently evidence fits a conclusion.

questions.stem: Which sentence is an objective summary of a team dividing work?
choices: Mara is selfish and Tomas is perfect.
This is the greatest story ever written.
Tomas deserves every possible prize.
Mara finishes the poster while Tomas leads the first hour.
questions.explanation: Saying that Mara finishes the poster while Tomas leads the first hour reports the arrangement without a personal evaluation.

questions.stem: A brief summary of The Repair Table should emphasize which development?
choices: Visitors’ questions turn the exhibition into a shared learning activity.
Every item on the supply list has a name.
A visitor stands near a particular shelf.
The tape could have been another color.
questions.explanation: The shared learning activity is the main development; incidental details can be omitted.

questions.stem: Which phrase signals an unsupported judgment in a summary?
choices: the finished poster
the foolish librarian
the first hour
the repair table
questions.explanation: Foolish evaluates the person; the other phrases identify ordinary source details.

questions.stem: A summary says Mara abandons the table without a plan. The text says she arranges coverage. What needs revision?
choices: All summaries must list every supply.
Objective summaries cannot mention a person.
The summary distorts an important event.
The text must be ignored to shorten it.
questions.explanation: Shortening should preserve important meaning, including the arrangement for coverage.

questions.stem: For a summary of the supply procedure, which detail becomes especially relevant?
choices: Mara’s model once had a crooked tower.
Tomas has a paper-arch photograph.
The whole neighborhood enjoys stories.
Supplies are labeled and adult-use tools stay with the librarian.
questions.explanation: A procedure summary needs the steps and conditions that make the procedure usable.

questions.stem: Which summary is too vague to be useful?
choices: People do things and learn.
Visitors ask questions, so the library adds a repair table.
Mara and Tomas divide the work around an earlier promise.
The poster becomes a record of visitors’ questions.
questions.explanation: The vague statement omits the specific situation and developments.

questions.stem: Why should a summary distinguish a character’s belief from a story’s events?
choices: All beliefs are exact quotations.
Reporting a belief does not establish that the belief is true.
Characters never have beliefs.
Summaries must agree with every character.
questions.explanation: A source may show a character believing something that later proves mistaken.

questions.stem: Which connection is supported: visitors ask how models work, and the librarian proposes a repair table in response?
choices: The visitors refused all help.
The request proves the table solves every problem.
The request helps explain the proposal.
The proposal occurred a year before the request.
questions.explanation: The proposal responds to the questions; the passage does not guarantee every later outcome.

questions.stem: Which actions improve an objective summary? Select all that apply.
choices: Preserve the main developments.
Remove personal praise or blame from the summary.
Invent a new ending to make it shorter.
Include every minor action regardless of purpose.
questions.explanation: A summary is selective and faithful; it does not invent or evaluate in place of reporting.

questions.stem: What term names the order of events: sequence or quotation?
questions.explanation: Sequence identifies the order of events.

questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning in this lesson.
choices: A shortened account of a text’s main ideas or important events
A summary that keeps personal judgment separate from source content
An event that changes the main situation or explains an important decision
The order in which events or steps occur
questions.explanation: summary: A shortened account of a text’s main ideas or important events; objective summary: A summary that keeps personal judgment separate from source content; major event: An event that changes the main situation or explains an important decision; sequence: The order in which events or steps occur.

questions.stem: A plan is “tentative” because members expect to revise it. What does tentative mean here?
choices: Not final
Guaranteed successful
Impossible to change
Extremely colorful
questions.explanation: The expectation of revision shows that the plan is not yet final.

questions.stem: “Unlike the rigid board, the flexible strip bent.” Which clue best explains flexible?
choices: The first letter of strip
The contrast with rigid and the action bent
The number of words in the sentence
The final period alone
questions.explanation: The contrast and action both support the meaning able to bend.

questions.stem: What does re- contribute to reread?
choices: Before
Against
Again
Without
questions.explanation: Reread means read again.

questions.stem: In “the first draft of the essay,” which meaning of draft fits?
choices: A current of air
A team’s selection process
A payment instruction
An early version
questions.explanation: Essay identifies a writing context, so an early version fits.

questions.stem: A dictionary lists several meanings. How should a reader choose?
choices: Match the meaning to the sentence and surrounding ideas.
Always copy the first meaning.
Choose the longest definition.
Choose whichever definition sounds amusing.
questions.explanation: A valid word meaning must also fit the current context.

questions.stem: “She was reluctant; she hesitated before agreeing.” Which replacement preserves reluctant here?
choices: Delighted
Hesitant
Certain
Rapid
questions.explanation: Hesitation supports reluctance, while the other replacements change the meaning.

questions.stem: Why is splitting uncle into un- and cle unhelpful?
choices: Word parts never provide clues.
Every word ending in e is a suffix.
Those are not meaningful parts of that word.
Every word begins with a prefix.
questions.explanation: Recognizing real word parts matters; superficial letter matches can mislead.

questions.stem: A precise description gives six strips, each folded twice. What does precise emphasize?
choices: The greatest possible length
A surprising rhyme
An unsupported opinion
Exact, specific detail
questions.explanation: The quantities demonstrate specificity, not merely length.

questions.stem: Which strategies help determine an unfamiliar word’s meaning? Select all that apply.
choices: Assume every word has only one meaning.
Treat matching initial letters as proof.
Test a proposed meaning in the sentence.
Use a nearby contrast or example as a clue.
questions.explanation: Testing and contextual clues help; one-sense assumptions and letter guesses do not establish meaning.

questions.stem: What prefix in reread means again? Give only the prefix.
questions.explanation: The prefix re- contributes the meaning again.

questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning in this lesson.
choices: The surrounding language and situation that help establish meaning
A meaningful word part added at the beginning of a base
A meaningful word part added at the end of a base
Information about a word, including meanings and often usage examples
questions.explanation: context: The surrounding language and situation that help establish meaning; prefix: A meaningful word part added at the beginning of a base; suffix: A meaningful word part added at the end of a base; reference entry: Information about a word, including meanings and often usage examples.

questions.stem: Dorothy is carried far from home and seeks advice about returning. What connects these events?
choices: Her journey has no goal.
Her new location creates a problem that motivates seeking guidance.
She already knows the route home.
The color of a road removes every obstacle.
questions.explanation: Being far from home helps explain why Dorothy seeks guidance.

questions.stem: Which observation analyzes setting rather than merely naming it?
choices: The story includes a road.
The story includes houses.
The unfamiliar country makes Dorothy depend on guidance.
The story includes Kansas.
questions.explanation: The observation about Dorothy depending on guidance explains how the unfamiliar place affects action.

questions.stem: The Scarecrow says he wants brains and joins the journey to Oz. What does this show directly?
choices: He can never solve a problem.
Every other character shares the same goal.
Oz has already granted his request.
His stated goal helps motivate his decision.
questions.explanation: The wish explains joining; it does not settle what his abilities are.

questions.stem: A character calls himself cowardly. What should a careful reader examine next?
choices: His actions across later situations
Only the title of the book
The actor in a film version
The number of letters in his name
questions.explanation: Actions may support or complicate a character’s self-description.

questions.stem: Which note shows a plot connection?
choices: The book has many paragraphs.
After Dorothy frees the Scarecrow, he can join her journey.
The Scarecrow has a name.
Chapter 3 follows chapter 2.
questions.explanation: The note explains a change caused by an event.

questions.stem: Why should an essay on Baum’s novel avoid relying on remembered film details?
choices: Films always copy every detail exactly.
Chapter references make reading unnecessary.
An adaptation can change the source’s details.
Novels have no settings.
questions.explanation: An analysis must use the assigned source; adaptations can differ.

questions.stem: Which statement identifies a goal rather than a setting?
choices: Dorothy is in Kansas at the opening.
The road passes through a forest.
The companions reach unfamiliar country.
Dorothy wants to return home.
questions.explanation: Wanting to return home identifies what drives Dorothy’s journey.

questions.stem: A log lists events but cannot explain why they matter. Which addition would help most?
choices: The change or consequence produced by each event
An invented prize for each character
A guess at every character’s age
The same opinion repeated after every chapter
questions.explanation: Recording consequences helps turn a list into plot analysis.

questions.stem: Which notes belong in a useful chapter log? Select all that apply.
choices: A character’s stated goal
A film event absent from the chapter
A made-up explanation presented as fact
An important event and its consequence
questions.explanation: A log preserves source evidence and connections; it should not substitute invented or adapted events.

questions.stem: What term names the time and place of a story?
questions.explanation: Setting includes time, place, and conditions.

questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning in this lesson.
choices: The time, place, and surrounding conditions of a story
The organized sequence of story events and their connections
A struggle involving obstacles or incompatible goals
A desire, reason, or pressure that drives a character’s action
questions.explanation: setting: The time, place, and surrounding conditions of a story; plot: The organized sequence of story events and their connections; conflict: A struggle involving obstacles or incompatible goals; motivation: A desire, reason, or pressure that drives a character’s action.

questions.stem: A character says he is unkind but repeatedly helps others. What should an analysis do?
choices: Treat the self-description as the only evidence.
Invent a reason that the text never suggests.
Explain the contrast between his self-description and behavior.
Ignore the helpful actions.
questions.explanation: The contrast is meaningful characterization and deserves explanation.

questions.stem: Which detail most directly shows considerate behavior?
choices: She wears a blue coat.
She is mentioned in chapter 2.
She has a short name.
She waits and helps another person finish.
questions.explanation: Waiting and helping show behavior relevant to consideration.

questions.stem: Which statement identifies an emotion rather than a lasting trait?
choices: He feels frightened during the crossing.
He regularly keeps promises.
He often considers others’ needs.
He repeatedly works through difficult problems.
questions.explanation: Fear during one crossing is a feeling in a particular situation.

questions.stem: The Tin Woodman helps a mouse while saying he has no heart. Which interpretation best fits that contrast?
choices: His speech makes his actions irrelevant.
Kindness is already visible in his actions.
The scene proves he never helps anyone.
The mouse is an ordinary mechanical part.
questions.explanation: Helping another creature provides evidence of concern despite his self-description.

questions.stem: Why include more than one scene in a claim about a character’s usual behavior?
choices: A character can appear in only one scene.
Repeated evidence removes the need for reasoning.
A pattern provides stronger support than one isolated action.
Two scenes always prove a lifelong trait.
questions.explanation: Multiple scenes can support a pattern, though the explanation and limits still matter.

questions.stem: “The reader recognizes courage the Lion has already shown” focuses on what?
choices: A change in the book’s publication date
A new physical setting only
A claim that fear never exists
A developing understanding of the character
questions.explanation: The sentence describes the reader’s recognition rather than necessarily a new ability.

questions.stem: Lena waits once while her brother ties his shoes. Which claim overstates the evidence?
choices: Lena is always patient in every situation.
Lena waits in this scene.
The scene shows one patient action.
Lena asks about the knot.
questions.explanation: One action cannot establish an exceptionless claim about all situations.

questions.stem: What is the best support for calling a character resourceful?
choices: Say every reader must agree.
Explain a scene where the character finds a workable solution.
Repeat the adjective three times.
Mention the character’s hair color.
questions.explanation: A trait label needs relevant behavior and an explanation.

questions.stem: Which details can contribute to characterization? Select all that apply.
choices: An invented scene treated as source evidence
A character’s words and choices
Another character’s response to those choices
A nickname treated as conclusive proof of every trait
questions.explanation: Words, choices, and responses help develop a character; invention and unchecked labels do not.

questions.stem: What term names the way a text develops a character?
questions.explanation: Characterization includes description, actions, speech, thought, and responses.

questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning in this lesson.
choices: How a text develops a character through details such as actions and speech
A relatively lasting quality suggested by a pattern of behavior
A feeling experienced in a particular situation
A meaningful change or deepening across a text
questions.explanation: characterization: How a text develops a character through details such as actions and speech; trait: A relatively lasting quality suggested by a pattern of behavior; emotion: A feeling experienced in a particular situation; development: A meaningful change or deepening across a text.

questions.stem: “I can help,” Tomas said. Mara watched him. What viewpoint is used outside the dialogue?
choices: First person because of the quoted I
Second person because Tomas speaks
No viewpoint can exist in dialogue
Third person
questions.explanation: The narration names Tomas and Mara; the quoted I belongs to a character’s speech.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes author and narrator?
choices: The author creates the text; the narrator is its telling voice.
The narrator must be the author in every story.
The author is always a fictional character.
Narrators can appear only in poems.
questions.explanation: Narration is a role inside the work, not automatically the author’s personal voice.

questions.stem: A first-person narrator sees Tomas watching but cannot hear his private thoughts. Which sentence respects that limit?
choices: Every visitor privately agreed with me.
Tomas watched me, and I wondered what he thought.
Tomas secretly knew the answer, though he never told me.
I knew every thought in Tomas’s mind without explanation.
questions.explanation: “Tomas watched me, and I wondered what he thought” reports an observation and the narrator’s own uncertainty.

questions.stem: Why does a later revelation about Oz affect an earlier scene?
choices: It proves characters knew the revelation all along.
It makes every detail irrelevant.
It provides new information for interpreting the earlier performance.
It erases the earlier scene from the book.
questions.explanation: Readers can reinterpret earlier evidence after learning more.

questions.stem: A narrator reports a character saying, “I never make mistakes.” What does that establish?
choices: The claim must be true.
The author never makes mistakes.
Every narrator agrees with every speaker.
The character makes that claim.
questions.explanation: Reporting speech establishes the speech, not necessarily its truth.

questions.stem: What must change when third-person access to two minds becomes a limited first-person account?
choices: Private knowledge outside the narrator’s access must be removed or explained.
Only the font must change.
All observations must disappear.
Every fact must become a question.
questions.explanation: Viewpoint determines access to information, not merely pronoun selection.

questions.stem: Which question best analyzes narrative perspective?
choices: How long is the author’s surname?
Whose thoughts does this passage allow the reader to know?
How many pages are in the edition?
What color is the cover?
questions.explanation: Access to thought and knowledge helps define narrative perspective.

questions.stem: You invent Dorothy’s thought while adapting a scene. How should you present it?
choices: Use it as proof of the original’s meaning.
Claim the original contains it without checking.
Label it as part of your creative adaptation.
Quote it as Baum’s exact wording.
questions.explanation: Creative additions are allowed in an adaptation but must not be mistaken for source evidence.

questions.stem: Which practices support accurate viewpoint analysis? Select all that apply.
choices: Check narration outside quotation marks.
Assume all third-person narration knows everything.
Track what each character knows at the time.
Treat later knowledge as available from the beginning.
questions.explanation: Viewpoint analysis depends on actual access to information and its timing.

questions.stem: What term names the telling voice of a story?
questions.explanation: The narrator is the voice that tells the story.

questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning in this lesson.
choices: The voice that tells a story
The position from which events are presented
A storyteller who participates using I or we
A storyteller who refers to characters using names or third-person pronouns
questions.explanation: narrator: The voice that tells a story; point of view: The position from which events are presented; first-person narrator: A storyteller who participates using I or we; third-person narrator: A storyteller who refers to characters using names or third-person pronouns.

questions.stem: Which is a topic rather than a theme statement?
choices: Friendship
Different strengths can make cooperation valuable.
People may underestimate abilities they already use.
A valued home can matter more than unfamiliar wonders.
questions.explanation: Friendship names a subject; the other choices express ideas about subjects.

questions.stem: What makes a whole-novel theme analysis stronger?
choices: A claim about every person in all situations
Evidence from several parts, including the ending
Only a favorite line with no explanation
A film scene absent from the novel
questions.explanation: A pattern across the work supports a larger interpretation.

questions.stem: “Dorothy travels to Oz” is primarily what?
choices: A quotation from every chapter
A source citation
A plot statement
A developed universal theme
questions.explanation: It names an event rather than a larger idea about experience.

questions.stem: A draft claims nobody needs help, but the plot repeatedly shows assistance. What should the writer do?
choices: Delete every scene involving help.
Insist that counterexamples do not matter.
Replace the novel with an invented ending.
Revise the theme claim to account for that evidence.
questions.explanation: A defensible interpretation must fit important details rather than discard them.

questions.stem: Two stories both include friends. What is needed for a meaningful comparison?
choices: Explain how each develops an idea through specific events.
Declare their meanings identical immediately.
Count the letters in friends.
Ignore differences in choices and outcomes.
questions.explanation: A shared topic alone does not establish the same theme.

questions.stem: Which wording appropriately presents a supported interpretation?
choices: One scene proves all people always behave this way.
This pattern suggests that others can help someone recognize a strength.
The author privately told me this is the only meaning.
Every reader must accept my idea without evidence.
questions.explanation: “This pattern suggests” presents a supported interpretation while leaving room for evidence-based discussion.

questions.stem: Which statement is too vague to guide a theme analysis?
choices: Confidence may lag behind demonstrated ability.
Returning home can remain important despite adventure.
Things happen.
Different strengths can support cooperation.
questions.explanation: Things happen does not identify a meaningful relationship or insight.

questions.stem: Why examine an early chapter and a late chapter together?
choices: To avoid reading the middle forever
To prove every character stays unchanged
To replace evidence with chapter numbers
To trace how an idea develops or changes across the work
questions.explanation: Comparing stages helps explain development, while middle evidence remains useful.

questions.stem: Which actions help test a proposed theme? Select all that apply.
choices: Use only an invented sequel.
Look for a pattern across multiple scenes.
Assume the first idea can never be revised.
Consider details that challenge the first wording.
questions.explanation: Testing uses the text’s patterns and challenges; interpretations can improve through revision.

questions.stem: What term names a larger idea developed by a literary work?
questions.explanation: A theme is an idea developed through the work, not merely its topic.

questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning in this lesson.
choices: A larger idea about experience developed by a literary work
A subject a text explores
A complete sentence expressing a testable interpretation of a larger idea
A connected understanding formed by bringing evidence or ideas together
questions.explanation: theme: A larger idea about experience developed by a literary work; topic: A subject a text explores; theme statement: A complete sentence expressing a testable interpretation of a larger idea; synthesis: A connected understanding formed by bringing evidence or ideas together.

questions.stem: A report describes question cards helping visitors ask and volunteers group questions. Which central idea fits?
choices: The only important fact is the sign’s color.
Question cards changed how help was requested and provided.
Every library must buy more chairs.
All repaired models became permanent.
questions.explanation: The central idea connects both participation and the volunteers’ response.

questions.stem: Four daily counts total 64 visits, and people may visit repeatedly. What can the total establish?
choices: All visitors were satisfied.
Every visitor repaired a model successfully.
There were 64 counted visits.
There were exactly 64 different people.
questions.explanation: The defined unit is visits, not unique people or successful repairs.

questions.stem: Which is a topic rather than a central idea?
choices: Written questions offered another way to participate.
Grouping questions changed the volunteers’ demonstrations.
A question-card system made shared confusion visible.
Library help tables
questions.explanation: Library help tables names a subject without stating a developed point.

questions.stem: Which detail best supports “the cards offered another way to participate”?
choices: Visitors could write before speaking to the group.
The report contains three paragraphs.
The last count is 19.
The building has a name.
questions.explanation: Writing before speaking directly explains the additional participation route.

questions.stem: What does grouping similar questions illustrate?
choices: Why no one needed instructions
How volunteers changed the way they provided help
How all visitors became expert builders
Why the first day must have been rainy
questions.explanation: The detail concretely develops a change in the help process.

questions.stem: The report says durability was not measured. Which conclusion should be avoided?
choices: Some visitors used written questions.
The report has limits on what it measures.
The cards proved that every repair lasted longer.
The volunteers tried question cards.
questions.explanation: The claimed improvement in durability is outside the evidence.

questions.stem: How can a reader test a proposed central idea?
choices: Choose the longest sentence automatically.
Use only the final number.
Ignore a paragraph that complicates it.
Check whether it explains major details across the passage.
questions.explanation: A useful central idea accounts for the passage’s development.

questions.stem: “The method changed” is followed by a concrete description of grouping cards. What is that description doing?
choices: Elaborating the broad statement
Removing every supporting detail
Changing the report into a poem
Proving all possible causes
questions.explanation: The concrete description explains what the broad statement means.

questions.stem: Which statements respect the fictional report’s evidence? Select all that apply.
choices: The counts describe visits, not necessarily different people.
The report describes a change in how questions were handled.
The counts prove that all visitors learned equally.
The report measures how long every repair lasted.
questions.explanation: Accurate interpretation preserves the counted unit and the report’s stated limits.

questions.stem: What term names the main point developed across an informational passage?
questions.explanation: The central or main idea connects the important details.

questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning in this lesson.
choices: The main point developed across an informational passage
A detail that explains, illustrates, or establishes a main point
A sentence that states a paragraph’s main idea
Added explanation or examples that develop an idea
questions.explanation: central idea: The main point developed across an informational passage; supporting detail: A detail that explains, illustrates, or establishes a main point; topic sentence: A sentence that states a paragraph’s main idea; elaboration: Added explanation or examples that develop an idea.

questions.stem: A paragraph moves from first Sunday to second, third, and fourth. What structure is most prominent?
choices: Unrelated descriptions
A list of synonyms
Chronological
Alphabetical definitions
questions.explanation: The organizing pattern follows time.

questions.stem: A passage identifies visitors’ difficulty asking questions, then introduces cards as a response. What structure fits?
choices: An alphabetical index
A rhyme scheme
A character list only
Problem and solution
questions.explanation: A difficulty is paired with an attempted response.

questions.stem: Why does a time-ordered list not prove a cause?
choices: An earlier event may not be what produced a later event.
Time order makes every detail false.
Chronology cannot contain facts.
Dates never matter in explanations.
questions.explanation: Sequence establishes order, while causation needs additional support.

questions.stem: A comparison of two signs is most useful when it examines what?
choices: Different standards chosen to favor one sign
The same features of both signs
The color of one and an unrelated story about the other
Only the writer’s favorite sign
questions.explanation: Shared comparison criteria let readers understand meaningful similarities and differences.

questions.stem: What does “The report does not show whether this helped every visitor” contribute?
choices: A new fictional character
A guarantee of universal success
A limit on the scope of the claim
Proof that nobody benefited
questions.explanation: The sentence prevents a stronger conclusion than the evidence allows.

questions.stem: Which question analyzes a sentence’s structural role?
choices: How many vowels does it contain?
Could it be printed in blue?
Is it the shortest sentence on the page?
Does it introduce a problem, give an example, or qualify a claim?
questions.explanation: Structural analysis asks what work a sentence does in the passage.

questions.stem: A text contains the word after once. What should a reader do before labeling the entire structure?
choices: Examine the relationships across the whole passage.
Declare every paragraph chronological.
Ignore all other signal words and ideas.
Treat after as proof of causation.
questions.explanation: One word is a clue, not a complete structural analysis.

questions.stem: Which revision best emphasizes a cause-and-effect connection?
choices: A volunteer liked the color blue.
Because the ink blurred when wet, volunteers covered the cards.
The cards existed on Sunday.
Cards and windows are objects.
questions.explanation: The sentence explicitly connects an observed condition with a response.

questions.stem: Which statements about structure are accurate? Select all that apply.
choices: One signal word always labels an entire article.
Time order automatically proves causation.
One article can combine more than one structure.
A structure should fit the writer’s purpose.
questions.explanation: Texts can combine relationships, and organization should serve a purpose; signal words and order are not proofs.

questions.stem: What term names organization that follows time order?
questions.explanation: Chronological organization follows the order of events.

questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning in this lesson.
choices: The organization of ideas and their relationships
Organization that follows time order
Organization that explains how events contribute to outcomes
Organization around a difficulty and a response
questions.explanation: text structure: The organization of ideas and their relationships; chronological structure: Organization that follows time order; cause-and-effect structure: Organization that explains how events contribute to outcomes; problem-and-solution structure: Organization around a difficulty and a response.

questions.stem: A student group asks decision-makers to test an evening hour. What is its main purpose?
choices: To narrate a fantasy adventure
To define every word in a dictionary
To report a completed year-long trial
To persuade them to consider a trial
questions.explanation: The request aims to influence a decision about a proposed trial.

questions.stem: 18 of 30 voluntary Saturday respondents prefer an evening option. Which claim is supported?
choices: 18 surveyed respondents expressed that preference.
Every resident wants evening access.
Evenings will certainly attract more visitors.
No one prefers Saturday.
questions.explanation: The evidence describes respondents, not all residents or future attendance.

questions.stem: Which source is best placed to confirm the room schedule in the packet?
choices: A survey question about favorite colors
The building coordinator with scheduling access
An anonymous slogan with no source
A fictional character from a novel
questions.explanation: Relevant access to scheduling information fits the specific question.

questions.stem: The coordinator knows the schedule but has no attendance trial data. What should a reader conclude?
choices: The schedule must be false.
No statement by the coordinator can be useful.
Schedule knowledge does not establish future demand.
The coordinator knows every future result.
questions.explanation: Credibility is tied to the question and available evidence.

questions.stem: Which analysis of perspective stays grounded in the messages?
choices: The coordinator secretly hates all students.
The student group intends to deceive everyone.
Every operational concern is dishonest.
The coordinator emphasizes staffing and closure requirements.
questions.explanation: The emphasis is visible in the text; the other claims invent motives.

questions.stem: Which word most clearly overstates the survey result in “Everyone demands evenings”?
choices: Everyone
Evenings
The implied topic of time
The plural ending alone
questions.explanation: Everyone expands a limited respondent group to an entire population.

questions.stem: Why can a source’s acknowledgment of a limitation be useful?
choices: It guarantees the source has no perspective.
It helps readers judge what the evidence can establish.
It automatically makes every claim false.
It replaces the need for evidence.
questions.explanation: Stated limits help readers avoid conclusions beyond the source’s scope.

questions.stem: Which additional evidence would directly help evaluate the proposed trial?
choices: An unrelated novel’s ending
The longest word in the proposal
Actual attendance and staffing records from the trial
The model bridge’s paint color
questions.explanation: Attendance and staffing records address the proposal’s practical questions.

questions.stem: Which practices help evaluate a source? Select all that apply.
choices: Check whether its knowledge fits the question.
Trust every claim because of a job title.
Treat every disagreement as dishonesty.
Distinguish observations from predictions.
questions.explanation: Evaluation depends on relevant knowledge and evidence, not blanket trust or attacks on motives.

questions.stem: What term names what a text tries to accomplish?
questions.explanation: Purpose identifies the text’s intended work for its audience.

questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning in this lesson.
choices: What a text is trying to accomplish for its audience
The position or outlook shaping a writer’s emphasis
A statement that can be supported or challenged
How much trust a source deserves for a specific information need
questions.explanation: purpose: What a text is trying to accomplish for its audience; perspective: The position or outlook shaping a writer’s emphasis; claim: A statement that can be supported or challenged; credibility: How much trust a source deserves for a specific information need.

questions.stem: Counts are 12, 18, 15, and 19. Which caption is accurate?
choices: The final count is higher than the first, with a dip in week 3.
The count rises every week.
The count falls every week.
Every week has exactly 19 visits.
questions.explanation: The sequence rises, falls, then rises; the endpoints alone do not show constant growth.

questions.stem: What does a table most directly contribute when it lists exact weekly counts?
choices: The identity of every visitor
Easy access to individual values
Proof of everyone’s feelings
A complete explanation of every cause
questions.explanation: A table presents values but does not automatically establish feelings, causes, or identity.

questions.stem: A photograph shows a crowded table at one moment. What can it establish by itself?
choices: Every visitor’s opinion
The number of different people all month
The arrangement and visible activity in that captured moment
The total attendance across four weeks
questions.explanation: One image records a limited time and frame.

questions.stem: Why compare visits with visits rather than visits with unique people?
choices: All numbers are interchangeable.
A larger number always uses the correct unit.
The wording never affects interpretation.
The units measure different things.
questions.explanation: Repeated visits and distinct people are different measurements.

questions.stem: A report says cards helped questions; another says supplies were hard to find. What is the best response?
choices: They may describe different aspects rather than contradict each other.
One source must be lying.
Both statements must be identical.
Neither statement can concern the same event.
questions.explanation: A process can have strengths and weaknesses at the same time.

questions.stem: Two websites repeat the same unsourced sentence. Why is that weak corroboration?
choices: A claim becomes certain after two copies.
They may share one unsupported origin.
Repetition always proves independence.
Websites cannot contain true information.
questions.explanation: Independent support requires more than duplicated wording.

questions.stem: A chart’s caption says new members, but its data count visits. What is wrong?
choices: Every visit creates a new member.
The chart no longer contains any numbers.
The caption changes the measured unit.
The caption is automatically clearer.
questions.explanation: Changing visits to new members creates a claim the data do not support.

questions.stem: Which question helps investigate an apparent discrepancy?
choices: Which source has the brightest color?
Which title is shorter?
Which writer has the longest name?
Do the sources use the same time period and definition?
questions.explanation: Scope and definitions can explain apparent differences.

questions.stem: Which practices support fair comparison across media? Select all that apply.
choices: Treat a vivid photograph as a complete attendance record.
Check units and time periods.
Explain what each form can and cannot show.
Assume matching wording means independent evidence.
questions.explanation: Matching scope and recognizing each medium’s limits support sound comparison.

questions.stem: What term names a difference between two accounts that needs explanation?
questions.explanation: A discrepancy is a difference to investigate.

questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning in this lesson.
choices: The form used to communicate information
A particular way information is shown or described
Supporting evidence from sources for the same claim
A difference between accounts or representations that needs explanation
questions.explanation: medium: The form used to communicate information; representation: A particular way information is shown or described; corroboration: Supporting evidence from sources for the same claim; discrepancy: A difference between accounts or representations that needs explanation.

questions.stem: Which narrative plan gives a character a meaningful choice?
choices: The ending introduces a solution with no connection to earlier events.
Inez admits a recording problem so her partner can help plan a new interview.
A stranger solves everything while Inez waits without acting.
The story lists unrelated objects.
questions.explanation: Admitting the problem changes what the partners can do next.

questions.stem: Which topic is most manageable for a short focused narrative?
choices: All photography throughout history
A list of every camera ever made
One moment when a wrong photograph must be corrected before a display
Every event in a person’s life
questions.explanation: One consequential event can be developed with detail in a short narrative.

questions.stem: What does orientation help the reader understand?
choices: The dictionary definition of every word
Every possible future event
Only the final grade for the story
Who is involved and what the initial situation is
questions.explanation: Orientation supplies the initial context needed to follow the action.

questions.stem: Which ending grows from the stated conflict of an unchecked recording?
choices: The partners complete a new interview and verify its audio.
A volcano appears and ends the story without connection.
The narrator lists favorite colors.
A new character awards a prize for an unrelated sport.
questions.explanation: The checked interview responds to the original problem and their actions.

questions.stem: Must a personal narrative reveal a private or upsetting experience?
choices: No; it must instead invent facts and call them real.
No; an ordinary comfortable event can be meaningful.
Yes; only painful events count.
Yes; privacy makes writing impossible.
questions.explanation: Narrative skill can be practiced with ordinary experience or honestly labeled fiction.

questions.stem: Why identify the intended audience during planning?
choices: To remove every unfamiliar idea
To avoid any revision
To judge what context and explanation the reader needs
To assume every reader has identical tastes
questions.explanation: Audience awareness helps determine necessary background and clarity.

questions.stem: Which question checks whether events are causally connected?
choices: Does every sentence contain the same number of words?
Are all characters given identical names?
Is the title the longest line?
Would changing this choice change what happens next?
questions.explanation: The question examines the effect of a character’s choice.

questions.stem: What distinguishes an intentional open ending from an unfinished draft?
choices: It deliberately leaves a meaningful uncertainty while resolving enough of the central action.
It stops at any random word.
It omits every consequence.
It never connects to the story’s problem.
questions.explanation: An open ending is shaped around a purpose rather than simply abandoned.

questions.stem: Which choices help focus a short narrative? Select all that apply.
choices: Select one meaningful event.
Include an entire biography regardless of relevance.
Connect a character’s decision with a consequence.
Add unrelated surprises instead of developing the conflict.
questions.explanation: Focus and connected consequences make the narrative coherent.

questions.stem: What term names information that establishes a story’s initial situation?
questions.explanation: Orientation establishes context at the beginning.

questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning in this lesson.
choices: A text that presents connected events involving characters or a speaker
Information that establishes the initial people, place, and situation
An event or choice that redirects the action
The result of the main struggle or the situation at the ending
questions.explanation: narrative: A text that presents connected events involving characters or a speaker; orientation: Information that establishes the initial people, place, and situation; turning point: An event or choice that redirects the action; resolution: The result of the main struggle or the situation at the ending.

questions.stem: Which detail best makes an uncomfortable pause concrete?
choices: Everything was nice.
The building existed somewhere.
The clock clicked while Inez held the silent recorder.
The room was very interesting.
questions.explanation: The specific sound and action help readers experience the pause.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly punctuates a statement followed by a dialogue tag?
choices: “I can call again” Arun said.
“I can call again, Arun said.”
I can call again,” Arun said.
“I can call again,” Arun said.
questions.explanation: The spoken words are enclosed, and the comma connects them to the tag.

questions.stem: When the speaker changes in standard narrative dialogue, what usually helps the reader?
choices: Start a new paragraph.
Remove all quotation marks.
Merge every speaker into one sentence.
Change the story’s tense at random.
questions.explanation: A new paragraph signals a new speaker.

questions.stem: Which is an action sentence rather than a dialogue tag?
choices: The librarian replied.
Inez placed the recorder on the table.
Inez said.
Arun asked.
questions.explanation: Placing the recorder is an action rather than a verb reporting speech.

questions.stem: What makes dialogue purposeful in a scene?
choices: It always uses the longest possible words.
It eliminates every descriptive sentence.
It reveals information, changes a relationship, or advances action.
It repeats everything without affecting the scene.
questions.explanation: Dialogue should contribute to the unfolding meaning or action.

questions.stem: Why might a writer summarize some moments instead of showing everything as a scene?
choices: Because scenes can never contain facts
Because summary is always more emotional
To avoid making any choices
To give space to the most important moments
questions.explanation: Narrative emphasis depends on selecting which moments deserve expansion.

questions.stem: Which question helps choose a sensory detail?
choices: What does this detail reveal or clarify in the scene?
Can I add an adjective to every noun?
Is it unrelated enough to surprise someone?
Does it force every reader to feel the same emotion?
questions.explanation: Purposeful details shape understanding rather than decorate randomly.

questions.stem: Which question-and-tag sentence is correctly punctuated?
choices: “Can we call again? Arun asked.”
“Can we call again?” Arun asked.
“Can we call again,” Arun asked?
Can we call again?” Arun asked.
questions.explanation: The question mark belongs to the spoken question inside the quotation marks.

questions.stem: Which revisions can improve a scene? Select all that apply.
choices: Add unrelated description to every sentence.
Replace a vague description with a relevant specific detail.
Repeat information without any narrative purpose.
Clarify who speaks when the speaker changes.
questions.explanation: Specific purposeful details and clear attribution help readers follow the scene.

questions.stem: What term names words such as Arun said that identify a speaker?
questions.explanation: A dialogue tag identifies who speaks.

questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning in this lesson.
choices: A particular narrative moment developed through action and detail
Description appealing to one or more senses
Spoken conversation represented in writing
Words identifying a speaker, such as she said or he asked
questions.explanation: scene: A particular narrative moment developed through action and detail; sensory detail: Description appealing to one or more senses; dialogue: Spoken conversation represented in writing; dialogue tag: Words identifying a speaker, such as she said or he asked.

questions.stem: Which sentence compresses a longer interval?
choices: Inez pressed Play and heard a hiss.
Arun held the card above the table.
The clock clicked before she answered.
They practiced for three afternoons.
questions.explanation: The sentence covers several days in a few words.

questions.stem: Which moment most deserves expansion in a story about admitting a mistake?
choices: The decision to tell the partner about the empty recording
Every routine pen-cap movement
The complete history of the desk
An unrelated walk months earlier
questions.explanation: The central choice affects the story’s conflict and consequence.

questions.stem: Why is “After the second microphone test” more specific than “Later”?
choices: It always makes a sentence shorter.
It identifies a relevant event that marks the time shift.
It proves every event has a cause.
It removes all need for context.
questions.explanation: The transition tells the reader what happened before the next action.

questions.stem: When is therefore an appropriate transition?
choices: Whenever a sentence is long
When the writer wants a word to sound formal
When the next idea follows as a result
Whenever two events happen near each other
questions.explanation: Therefore signals consequence, which needs a supported relationship.

questions.stem: Which ending shows a connected change in Inez’s behavior?
choices: A stranger announces an unrelated sports result.
The story stops in the middle of a word.
The narrator lists every kind of microphone.
She listens to a test clip before beginning the new interview.
questions.explanation: Checking the clip responds to the earlier failure to verify recording.

questions.stem: Can a quiet pause be important to pacing?
choices: Yes, if it develops a consequential hesitation or choice.
No, only running can create a scene.
No, every pause must be deleted.
Yes, but only if it includes a chase.
questions.explanation: Pacing concerns narrative emphasis, not just physical speed.

questions.stem: What should compression avoid removing?
choices: Unnecessary supply-list detail
A turning point needed to understand the outcome
Routine movements with no special role
Repeated statements of the same idea
questions.explanation: Readers need important choices and consequences even when routine time is shortened.

questions.stem: Which revision best avoids an overpromising ending?
choices: Every problem in the world is solved.
No recording can ever fail again.
Inez adopts a checking habit for the next interview.
Inez will never make any mistake again.
questions.explanation: A specific changed practice is more defensible than a perfect future.

questions.stem: Which techniques can improve pacing? Select all that apply.
choices: Summarize a routine interval.
Expand a meaningful decision with selected detail.
Give every action the same amount of space regardless of importance.
Remove all consequences from the ending.
questions.explanation: Pacing uses selective expansion and compression while preserving meaning.

questions.stem: What term names a narrative’s speed and allocation of emphasis?
questions.explanation: Pacing is how a narrative controls speed and emphasis.

questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning in this lesson.
choices: The speed and emphasis with which a narrative presents events
Narrative treatment that expands a particular moment
A compressed account of a longer interval or less central events
Language connecting parts by time, place, or relationship
questions.explanation: pacing: The speed and emphasis with which a narrative presents events; scene time: Narrative treatment that expands a particular moment; narrative summary: A compressed account of a longer interval or less central events; transition: Language connecting parts by time, place, or relationship.

questions.stem: Which change is primarily revision of organization?
choices: Move the admission before the plan it causes.
Correct one misspelled word.
Add a missing quotation mark.
Capitalize a sentence’s first letter.
questions.explanation: Moving events to clarify their relationship changes organization.

questions.stem: Which comment gives useful feedback?
choices: I dislike it for no stated reason.
I lost track of what it refers to in the second paragraph.
This is bad.
Make everything perfect.
questions.explanation: Specific feedback identifies a location and a reader difficulty.

questions.stem: A story’s central conflict is unclear. What should the writer prioritize?
choices: Adding random adjectives
Making the title longer
Clarifying the goal and obstacle
Changing every comma first
questions.explanation: Meaning and focus need attention before surface polishing can solve the problem.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of a revision memo?
choices: Claim every suggestion was wrong
Replace the revised story entirely
List only the number of keystrokes
Explain important changes and how they serve the reader
questions.explanation: A memo makes the writer’s revision decisions and reasons visible.

questions.stem: A reader suggests a new ending that changes your intended meaning. What is a reasonable response?
choices: Consider the concern and choose a repair that fits the purpose.
Accept every suggestion automatically.
Reject all feedback forever.
Pretend the reader never commented.
questions.explanation: The writer uses feedback thoughtfully while retaining responsibility for decisions.

questions.stem: Why recheck pronouns after cutting a paragraph?
choices: Cutting text always fixes every reference.
Their referents may no longer be clear.
Pronouns become forbidden after revision.
Every pronoun must become a noun in all writing.
questions.explanation: Changes in nearby context can create unclear references.

questions.stem: Which action is primarily editing?
choices: Reorder the whole plot.
Develop a missing turning-point scene.
Correct a missing closing quotation mark.
Choose a new central conflict.
questions.explanation: The quotation-mark correction addresses a convention.

questions.stem: Which statement about revision is accurate?
choices: Every revision must increase word count.
Adding adjectives is the only revision method.
Revision never changes ideas.
A useful revision can shorten a draft while improving its focus.
questions.explanation: Removing distractions can strengthen the intended meaning.

questions.stem: Which actions support a thoughtful revision process? Select all that apply.
choices: Measure success only by added words.
Treat punctuation correction as the solution to every plot problem.
Keep a before-and-after excerpt.
Explain how a change helps the intended reader.
questions.explanation: Visible changes and reader-focused reasons demonstrate revision more clearly than length alone.

questions.stem: What term names correcting spelling and punctuation?
questions.explanation: Editing addresses conventions; revision can also change larger meaning and structure.

questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning in this lesson.
choices: Changes to ideas, organization, development, or expression to improve a piece
Correction of conventions such as spelling and punctuation
Information about a reader’s experience and possible improvements
An explanation of why a change serves the writing’s purpose
questions.explanation: revision: Changes to ideas, organization, development, or expression to improve a piece; editing: Correction of conventions such as spelling and punctuation; feedback: Information about a reader’s experience and possible improvements; revision rationale: An explanation of why a change serves the writing’s purpose.

questions.topic: A debatable claim and focused reasons
questions.stem: Which claim fits a packet about a four-Thursday trial?
choices: Every schedule problem has been solved permanently.
Run the four-week trial if the required staffing is arranged.
Every library must remain open all night forever.
All residents have already attended the trial.
questions.explanation: The bounded claim matches the proposed duration and known staffing condition.

questions.topic: A debatable claim and focused reasons
questions.stem: Which statement is a reason rather than a restatement of “delay approval”?
choices: Approval should be delayed because it should wait.
Delay means not approving yet.
The required staffing plan is not yet ready.
Waiting is the best because delay is good.
questions.explanation: An unmet requirement explains why the writer proposes delay.

questions.topic: A debatable claim and focused reasons
questions.stem: What makes a claim debatable?
choices: It must insult someone.
It cannot use evidence.
It must be impossible to investigate.
Reasonable readers could question the position.
questions.explanation: Debatable claims permit reasoned disagreement and evaluation.

questions.topic: A debatable claim and focused reasons
questions.stem: Why is “everyone wants evenings” too broad for 30 voluntary survey responses?
choices: The evidence does not represent every person.
Thirty responses always equal the entire community.
Volunteers cannot express preferences.
Evenings cannot be discussed in writing.
questions.explanation: A limited sample supports claims about respondents, not everyone.

questions.topic: A debatable claim and focused reasons
questions.stem: Which pair contains distinct reasons?
choices: I like it; it is my favorite.
Evening interest exists; a limited trial can gather attendance data.
It is good; it is excellent.
We should do it; doing it is best.
questions.explanation: Evening interest and gathering attendance data give distinct reasons, unlike pairs that repeat approval.

questions.topic: A debatable claim and focused reasons
questions.stem: How should an argument handle a relevant fact that complicates its position?
choices: Pretend it supports the opposite of what it says.
Attack the person who noticed it.
Address it and adjust the claim if needed.
Erase it from the source.
questions.explanation: Reasoned argument accounts for relevant evidence, including complications.

questions.topic: A debatable claim and focused reasons
questions.stem: Which claim gives a reader the clearest proposed action?
choices: Improve everything somehow.
Make things better forever.
Do the best possible thing.
Add written question cards beside each model at the next event.
questions.explanation: A specific action, location, and timeframe make the recommendation understandable.

questions.topic: A debatable claim and focused reasons
questions.stem: What should determine a student argument’s evaluation in this module?
choices: Reasoning, evidence, fairness, and clarity
Agreement with one required opinion
The loudness of the writer’s anger
The number of insults included
questions.explanation: The task evaluates the quality of support, not conformity to a preferred position.

questions.topic: A debatable claim and focused reasons
questions.stem: Which choices strengthen an argument plan? Select all that apply.
choices: State the decision’s actual limits.
Repeat the same approval in different adjectives.
Promise permanent success without outcome evidence.
Use reasons that contribute different support.
questions.explanation: Clear scope and distinct reasons make an argument assessable.

questions.topic: A debatable claim and focused reasons
questions.stem: What term names the boundary of a claim?
questions.explanation: Scope identifies what the claim does and does not cover.

questions.topic: A debatable claim and focused reasons
questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning in this lesson.
choices: Reasons and evidence used to support a position
A position that reasonable readers could question or dispute
An explanation of why a position should be accepted
The boundary of what a statement or inquiry covers
questions.explanation: argument: Reasons and evidence used to support a position; debatable claim: A position that reasonable readers could question or dispute; reason: An explanation of why a position should be accepted; scope: The boundary of what a statement or inquiry covers.

questions.stem: Why is the survey relevant to a possible evening trial?
choices: It confirms that volunteers are trained.
It measures the room’s closing procedure.
It shows expressed interest among some current visitors.
It proves every resident will attend.
questions.explanation: The survey addresses expressed preference, not attendance or operations.

questions.stem: Which sentence supplies reasoning rather than merely repeating data?
choices: Eighteen respondents means eighteen respondents.
The survey contains responses.
A number is a number.
The interest gives a reason to test actual attendance before a permanent change.
questions.explanation: The sentence explains an implication for the decision while preserving uncertainty.

questions.stem: Which fact is most relevant to room availability?
choices: The coordinator confirms four available Thursdays.
The poster uses blue ink.
A model has a crooked tower.
A character in a novel wants courage.
questions.explanation: The schedule confirmation directly addresses availability.

questions.stem: What is missing from “These facts prove my point”?
choices: A longer title for the paragraph
An explanation of how the facts support the claim
An insult directed at opponents
A guarantee that every reader agrees
questions.explanation: Reasoning must make the connection explicit.

questions.stem: Which condition is most checkable?
choices: Approve if people are nice.
Approve whenever it feels perfect.
Approve only after an entrance volunteer and closing duties are assigned.
Approve if everything is fine.
questions.explanation: Specific assignments can be verified; vague descriptions cannot guide a decision reliably.

questions.stem: Why might a preference survey be insufficient for a permanent schedule change?
choices: Surveys can never provide any information.
Every preference is false.
Permanent decisions need no evidence.
Preferences alone do not establish actual use or ongoing feasibility.
questions.explanation: The survey contributes information but does not answer every necessary question.

questions.stem: Which claim is directly supported by 18 of 30 respondents choosing evenings?
choices: Some respondents preferred an evening option.
Every respondent preferred evenings.
All nonrespondents prefer evenings.
Every Thursday will have 18 visitors.
questions.explanation: The observed responses establish a bounded preference statement.

questions.stem: A writer includes a precise fact unrelated to the claim. What is the main problem?
choices: A fact’s wording never matters.
Precision does not make the fact relevant.
All precise facts are false.
Every argument needs unrelated facts.
questions.explanation: Relevance depends on the connection to the conclusion, not exactness alone.

questions.stem: Which actions strengthen an evidence paragraph? Select all that apply.
choices: Replace explanation with a declaration of victory.
Explain why a fact matters to the claim.
State an important limit on what the fact establishes.
Convert preferences into guaranteed future actions.
questions.explanation: A strong paragraph connects and qualifies evidence instead of overstating it.

questions.stem: What term names the explanation linking evidence to a claim?
questions.explanation: Reasoning supplies the connection between support and conclusion.

questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning in this lesson.
choices: Evidence that directly bears on the claim under discussion
The explanation connecting evidence with a conclusion
Enough appropriate evidence for a claim’s strength and scope
A limit or condition that makes a statement fit what is known
questions.explanation: relevant evidence: Evidence that directly bears on the claim under discussion; reasoning: The explanation connecting evidence with a conclusion; sufficient support: Enough appropriate evidence for a claim’s strength and scope; qualification: A limit or condition that makes a statement fit what is known.

questions.stem: A volunteer supports the event but needs a known ending time. Which paraphrase is fair?
choices: The volunteer hates all exhibitions.
The volunteer refuses every possible task.
The volunteer wants the library permanently closed.
The volunteer wants clear shift information before committing.
questions.explanation: The fair paraphrase preserves both support and the specific condition.

questions.stem: What is a concession in an argument?
choices: Acknowledging a valid point in another position
Insulting the other writer
Repeating the original claim without change
Inventing a weaker opponent
questions.explanation: A concession recognizes a point worth taking seriously.

questions.stem: Which response addresses an unclear closing schedule?
choices: Change the poster’s color.
Publish duties and departure times before recruiting.
Repeat survey numbers without discussing hours.
Call the volunteer lazy.
questions.explanation: A clear schedule directly responds to the practical concern.

questions.stem: What should a writer do if a counterclaim reveals a serious unresolved problem?
choices: Misquote the concern.
Declare that evidence no longer matters.
Reconsider, narrow, or delay the original recommendation.
Ignore the problem to appear confident.
questions.explanation: A responsible argument can change in response to a real weakness.

questions.stem: Why is “Volunteers hate visitors” an unfair version of a scheduling concern?
choices: It includes too much accurate evidence.
It states the closing time exactly.
It is a neutral summary of shift information.
It invents a hostile motive instead of representing the request.
questions.explanation: The invented motive changes the other person’s position.

questions.stem: A concern is that displayed cards may reveal private information. Which response is relevant?
choices: Review cards for identifying details before display.
Make the board larger without reviewing content.
Publish every card unchanged immediately.
Argue about the number of chairs.
questions.explanation: Reviewing identifying details addresses the privacy issue.

questions.stem: Must fairness mean all positions are equally well supported?
choices: No; it means insulting unsupported claims.
No; describe positions accurately, then evaluate their evidence.
Yes; every claim has identical support.
Yes; evidence must be ignored.
questions.explanation: Fair description and evidence-based evaluation are compatible.

questions.stem: What is the best test of whether a counterclaim section is meaningful?
choices: It repeats the writer’s favorite adjective.
It avoids every condition and uncertainty.
It addresses a real concern that matters to the decision.
It chooses the weakest imaginable objection.
questions.explanation: A meaningful challenge tests the argument rather than providing an easy target.

questions.stem: Which responses show fair argument? Select all that apply.
choices: Acknowledge a valid scheduling concern.
Invent hostile motives for the other side.
Revise a condition when evidence shows a gap.
Answer a staffing issue with an unrelated insult.
questions.explanation: Acknowledgment and relevant revision address the actual disagreement.

questions.stem: What term means acknowledging a valid point in another position?
questions.explanation: A concession recognizes a valid concern or point.

questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning in this lesson.
choices: A position that challenges the writer’s claim
Acknowledgment of a valid point in another position
An explanation addressing a challenge to an argument
An accurate restatement of another idea in the writer’s own words
questions.explanation: counterclaim: A position that challenges the writer’s claim; concession: Acknowledgment of a valid point in another position; response: An explanation addressing a challenge to an argument; fair paraphrase: An accurate restatement of another idea in the writer’s own words.

questions.stem: An essay begins with a four-week trial but ends by demanding permanent hours without new support. What needs revision?
choices: The claim’s scope is inconsistent.
The essay has too many accurate citations.
The trial must be renamed a novel.
All conclusions must be removed.
questions.explanation: The recommendation changes beyond the evidence developed in the essay.

questions.stem: Which transition fits a genuine contrast?
choices: First, for a final unrelated point
However
For the same reason, when no reason is shared
Therefore, when no result follows
questions.explanation: However signals a contrast when the ideas actually differ.

questions.stem: Which conclusion stays within the packet’s evidence?
choices: Every library must adopt permanent hours immediately.
No future records are needed because success is guaranteed.
Try the four dates after staffing is arranged, then examine attendance before extending.
The trial has already made every resident happy.
questions.explanation: The bounded recommendation preserves the conditions and the need for actual results.

questions.stem: Why read only paragraph-opening sentences during revision?
choices: To avoid checking evidence ever again
To prove that sentence length determines truth
To replace the full essay with headings
To check the overall sequence and roles of the paragraphs
questions.explanation: This pass helps reveal the argument’s structure; other passes still check detail.

questions.stem: Which sentence most clearly connects evidence with a trial recommendation?
choices: Expressed interest supports testing attendance, although preferences may not become visits.
Interest is interesting because interest exists.
Therefore, blue signs are popular.
Everyone agrees with everything.
questions.explanation: The sentence explains both the implication and limit of the evidence.

questions.stem: What should an argument conclusion avoid introducing as fact?
choices: A reminder of an important condition
Unverified trial results absent from the evidence
A concise restatement of the bounded recommendation
A relevant next step
questions.explanation: A conclusion cannot create new results that the source packet never supplies.

questions.stem: What makes “This proves it” weak when several ideas precede it?
choices: Every short sentence is forbidden.
Pronouns are always incorrect.
The reference and reasoning may be unclear.
The sentence contains a capital letter.
questions.explanation: Readers need to know what this and it refer to and why the evidence supports the claim.

questions.stem: Which feedback question is most useful?
choices: Do you agree with me regardless of the facts?
Can you praise every sentence?
Can you ignore the difficult paragraph?
Where does my conclusion become stronger than my evidence?
questions.explanation: The specific question invites evaluation of a reasoning problem.

questions.stem: Which checks belong in argument revision? Select all that apply.
choices: Replace every qualification with a guarantee.
Confirm that factual claims have support.
Add a new unsupported result to the conclusion.
Check that the response addresses the actual opposing concern.
questions.explanation: Evidence and fair response checks improve the argument’s reliability.

questions.stem: What term names the connected flow among sentences and ideas?
questions.explanation: Cohesion helps the reader follow the relationships in the writing.

questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning in this lesson.
choices: The opening that provides context and the direction of a piece
The connected flow among sentences and ideas
A purposeful ending that draws together the developed reasoning
Improving a position’s support, organization, clarity, and fairness
questions.explanation: introduction: The opening that provides context and the direction of a piece; cohesion: The connected flow among sentences and ideas; conclusion: A purposeful ending that draws together the developed reasoning; argument revision: Improving a position’s support, organization, clarity, and fairness.

questions.stem: What sound pattern appears in “Small, slow steps”?
choices: A change of speaker
Alliteration of the initial s sound
A comparison using like
A complete rhyme scheme by itself
questions.explanation: The nearby words repeat the initial s sound.

questions.stem: Which detail appeals most directly to hearing?
choices: A crooked handle points homeward.
Two shoulders share the shelter.
Rain ticks against the window glass.
A red umbrella stands at the door.
questions.explanation: Ticks evokes a brief repeated sound.

questions.stem: What is the poem’s speaker?
choices: Necessarily the author’s real-life childhood self
The person who printed the book
Every reader at the same time
The voice presented in the poem
questions.explanation: The speaker is a textual voice and need not equal the author.

questions.stem: Which analysis explains imagery’s effect rather than merely naming it?
choices: The patch makes repair visible, preparing for the umbrella’s continued use.
The poem contains imagery.
There are words on the page.
The title has three words.
questions.explanation: Connecting the visible patch with the umbrella’s continued use explains the image’s contribution.

questions.stem: What can “ticks” contribute in a rain scene?
choices: A guarantee that the rain is dangerous
A suggestion of the sound against glass
Proof of an exact rainfall amount
The owner’s full biography
questions.explanation: The word evokes sound, not measurement or biography.

questions.stem: Why should a reader avoid claiming the author owned this exact umbrella?
choices: Speakers never observe scenes.
Authors cannot invent details.
The poem does not provide that biographical evidence.
Poems cannot mention objects.
questions.explanation: An invented speaker or scene cannot establish the author’s personal history.

questions.stem: Must every poem rhyme?
choices: Yes; otherwise no imagery is possible.
Yes; every line must end with the same word.
No; but poems must avoid sound entirely.
No; poems can create patterns and meaning without rhyme.
questions.explanation: Poetry can use many forms, including free verse.

questions.stem: Which question best helps explain a detail’s effect?
choices: What becomes less clear or meaningful if the detail is removed?
How can I count every letter?
Can I assign a secret code without evidence?
Must every reader feel exactly what I feel?
questions.explanation: The removal test focuses attention on the detail’s contribution.

questions.stem: Which statements are supported methods for reading poetry? Select all that apply.
choices: Distinguish the speaker from the author.
Connect a sound pattern with the surrounding scene.
Assume a repeated letter always makes the same sound.
Treat a personal interpretation as the only possible answer without evidence.
questions.explanation: Poetry analysis attends to voice, actual sounds, context, and supported interpretations.

questions.stem: What term names a poem’s presented voice?
questions.explanation: The speaker is the voice within the poem.

questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning in this lesson.
choices: Language that evokes sensory experience
The voice presented in a poem
Repetition of an initial consonant sound in nearby words
Use of words that suggest sounds
