questions.explanation: imagery: Language that evokes sensory experience; speaker: The voice presented in a poem; alliteration: Repetition of an initial consonant sound in nearby words; onomatopoeia: Use of words that suggest sounds.

questions.stem: Which sentence contains a simile?
choices: The line has twelve people.
The table stands near the door.
The line curled like a ribbon around the table.
I like reading at the table.
questions.explanation: “The line curled like a ribbon around the table” compares the line and ribbon through their curving shape.

questions.stem: “A forest folded into sleeves” describes umbrellas. What is the figure doing?
choices: Claiming umbrellas literally grow roots
Giving an attendance count
Naming a real forest’s address
Comparing grouped umbrellas with a forest
questions.explanation: The metaphor transfers a relevant visual relationship, not every literal forest feature.

questions.stem: Which word most strongly suggests an object is no longer useful?
choices: Ruined
Repaired
Restored
Mended
questions.explanation: Ruined commonly suggests loss of usable condition, unlike the restoration words.

questions.stem: Why might repaired fit an umbrella that still shelters people?
choices: It guarantees every repair lasts forever.
It emphasizes restored usefulness.
It proves the umbrella never had damage.
It means the umbrella is a tree.
questions.explanation: The word connects prior work with present usefulness without denying earlier damage.

questions.stem: Does “I like the poem” contain a simile?
choices: Yes; the poem becomes a person.
No; similes cannot appear in sentences.
No; like expresses preference here.
Yes; every use of like is a comparison.
questions.explanation: The grammatical use matters; preference is not a comparison between two things.

questions.stem: What should a metaphor analysis identify?
choices: Every unrelated fact about either object
Only the number of letters
A literal identity between all their features
The compared things and the relevant shared quality
questions.explanation: A figure usually transfers selected qualities, not complete identity.

questions.stem: The poem contrasts a small table with a journey that continues. Which interpretation fits?
choices: Imagination can extend beyond the immediate physical space.
A highway physically grows through the room.
The table becomes larger than a city.
The drawing proves a historical expedition occurred.
questions.explanation: The contrast supports imaginative extension rather than literal transformation.

questions.stem: Why examine context when discussing connotation?
choices: Context removes all differences between words.
Associations can change with usage and situation.
Words have no associations at all.
Every word makes every reader feel exactly the same.
questions.explanation: Connotation is influenced by how and where a word is used.

questions.stem: Which statements describe careful figurative analysis? Select all that apply.
choices: Every word like creates a simile.
A metaphor requires all literal features to match.
A comparison usually transfers selected qualities.
Nearby context helps test the interpretation.
questions.explanation: Figures depend on selective relationships and contextual support.

questions.stem: What term names an explicit comparison often using like or as?
questions.explanation: A simile makes an explicit comparison.

questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning in this lesson.
choices: Language extending beyond a literal sense for comparison or emphasis
An explicit comparison, often using like or as
A comparison presenting one thing in terms of another
Associations or feelings a word can carry beyond its basic definition
questions.explanation: figurative language: Language extending beyond a literal sense for comparison or emphasis; simile: An explicit comparison, often using like or as; metaphor: A comparison presenting one thing in terms of another; connotation: Associations or feelings a word can carry beyond its basic definition.

questions.stem: What groups lines of a poem, often with a blank line separating groups?
choices: A dialogue tag
A bibliography
A survey sample
A stanza
questions.explanation: A stanza is a group of verse lines.

questions.stem: The end words are away, stay, door, floor, string, wing. What rhyme pattern fits?
choices: AABBCC
ABCABC
AAAAAA
ABCDAB
questions.explanation: Each adjacent pair shares ending sounds, while the three pairs differ.

questions.stem: Must a reader make a long pause at every line break?
choices: No; line breaks can never affect emphasis.
No; sentence grammar also guides the reading.
Yes; every line is always a complete sentence.
Yes; punctuation should be ignored.
questions.explanation: A thought may continue across a line break, though the break can still affect emphasis.

questions.stem: Which statement about free verse is accurate?
choices: It must use a strict AABB pattern.
It cannot contain imagery.
It can use deliberate rhythm and repetition without a fixed scheme.
It has no possible structure.
questions.explanation: Free verse is not the absence of craft or pattern.

questions.stem: Why is “the last stanza comes last” weak analysis?
choices: It gives too much evidence about meaning.
It proves the poem has no ending.
It correctly explains every structural effect.
It names location without explaining the stanza’s contribution.
questions.explanation: Structural analysis needs the role or effect, not just position.

questions.stem: What should determine whether two words rhyme?
choices: Their ending sounds
Only their first letters
Their word lengths alone
Their positions in the alphabet
questions.explanation: Rhyme concerns sound correspondence rather than appearance alone.

questions.stem: What can rearranging the same words into different lines help a writer explore?
choices: A requirement to add unrelated facts
Changes in emphasis and pacing
Proof that every arrangement has identical effect
The publication date of the poem
questions.explanation: Arrangement can alter how readers encounter words and ideas.

questions.stem: A forced rhyme changes the intended meaning. What is a sensible revision?
choices: Delete every image from the poem.
Claim the altered meaning was in the source all along.
Change the wording or form to preserve the intended meaning.
Keep it because rhyme always outranks meaning.
questions.explanation: Form should serve the poem’s purpose rather than override it accidentally.

questions.stem: Which practices support form analysis? Select all that apply.
choices: Explain what a stanza contributes to development.
Treat blank lines as spoken words.
Assume every free-verse poem is unplanned.
Identify rhyme patterns by sound.
questions.explanation: Stanza roles and sound relationships are meaningful formal evidence.

questions.stem: What term names poetry without a fixed regular meter or rhyme scheme?
questions.explanation: Free verse can still use intentional rhythm, imagery, and repetition.

questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning in this lesson.
choices: The point where one line of verse ends and another begins
A grouped set of lines in a poem
A correspondence of ending sounds
Poetry without a fixed regular meter or rhyme scheme
questions.explanation: line break: The point where one line of verse ends and another begins; stanza: A grouped set of lines in a poem; rhyme: A correspondence of ending sounds; free verse: Poetry without a fixed regular meter or rhyme scheme.

questions.stem: Which line is a stage direction?
choices: [Maya turns the card face down.]
MAYA. Nobody has a question.
ELI. Try writing one.
MAYA. Then why didn’t they ask?
questions.explanation: Brackets mark an action instruction outside the dialogue in this script.

questions.stem: What supports an inference that Maya worries about embarrassment?
choices: The script has capital letters.
She hides the card and asks whether everyone else knows the answer.
The scene includes a library room only.
Eli has a short name.
questions.explanation: The action and question together support the inferred concern.

questions.stem: Must a performer speak every stage direction aloud?
choices: Yes; characters cannot move otherwise.
No; directions must always be ignored.
No; directions usually guide action rather than dialogue.
Yes; every bracketed word is a spoken line.
questions.explanation: Stage directions generally tell performers what to do or establish, not what to say.

questions.stem: What is added by a performance of a script?
choices: Proof that no other interpretation is possible
The author’s exact private thoughts
A guarantee of audience agreement
Specific timing, voice, and movement choices
questions.explanation: Performance supplies choices beyond the written words.

questions.stem: When adapting a private thought into drama, what should a writer consider?
choices: How action, dialogue, or a deliberate monologue can convey it
How to keep every thought invisible without explanation
How to claim new lines are exact source quotations
How to remove all character motivation
questions.explanation: Drama needs a way for the audience to encounter the information.

questions.stem: Which comparison between prose and drama is analytical?
choices: All forms communicate in exactly the same way.
Prose states the worry; the script suggests it through a hidden recorder and a question.
Drama is always better.
Prose is always boring.
questions.explanation: Comparing a directly stated worry with a hidden recorder and a question explains different ways to convey the same information.

questions.stem: What does subtext refer to?
choices: Every word in a bibliography
The actor’s name on a poster
Meaning or pressure suggested beneath the spoken words
The page number printed at the bottom
questions.explanation: Subtext concerns implied meaning, supported by context and action.

questions.stem: A performer adds a long pause not specified in the script. How should it be described?
choices: A word-for-word quotation from the script
The only possible correct performance
Evidence of a new source author
A performance choice that may be supported by the scene
questions.explanation: A pause can be a reasonable interpretation without being explicitly required.

questions.stem: Which actions support fair comparison of script and performance? Select all that apply.
choices: Treat all performance additions as original written words.
Distinguish required directions from added delivery choices.
Explain how a pause or movement changes emphasis.
Assume louder delivery is always more meaningful.
questions.explanation: Fair comparison separates source evidence from performance choices and explains their effects.

questions.stem: What term names a work reshaped for another form?
questions.explanation: An adaptation changes form or purpose while drawing on an earlier work.

questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning in this lesson.
choices: A work designed for performance by speakers or actors
A script instruction describing action, setting, or delivery
A work reshaped for another form or purpose
Unstated meaning or pressure suggested beneath spoken words
questions.explanation: drama: A work designed for performance by speakers or actors; stage direction: A script instruction describing action, setting, or delivery; adaptation: A work reshaped for another form or purpose; subtext: Unstated meaning or pressure suggested beneath spoken words.

questions.stem: Which is a focused research question that avoids assuming a result?
choices: What is everything about every library?
What do the four-week records show, and what remains unknown?
Why are all evening trials always successful?
Why does everyone dislike libraries?
questions.explanation: The question is bounded and leaves the conclusion open to evidence.

questions.stem: Which packet source directly records weekly visits?
choices: An unrelated poem
A proposed slogan without data
R1, the attendance record
R2, the closing notes
questions.explanation: R1 provides the defined weekly attendance counts.

questions.stem: For research on the trial’s recorded operations, what kind of source is the volunteer’s closing log?
choices: Necessarily a perfect source
A fictional novel about another topic
A dictionary entry only
A primary source
questions.explanation: The log directly records the event, although it still has limits.

questions.stem: A later article interprets the trial records. For investigating the trial, it is generally what?
choices: A secondary source
A direct attendance measurement itself
An automatic replacement for the records
Proof that the records cannot contain errors
questions.explanation: The article discusses and interprets existing evidence.

questions.stem: Do primary sources automatically avoid error or bias?
choices: No; therefore none can be useful.
No; their methods and limits still need examination.
Yes; direct records cannot be mistaken.
Yes; authorship removes every uncertainty.
questions.explanation: Direct evidence can be valuable and still require evaluation.

questions.stem: What should a researcher do when a needed number is absent?
choices: Borrow an unrelated number without explanation.
Claim the gap proves the preferred answer.
Identify the gap and the evidence needed to fill it.
Invent a plausible number.
questions.explanation: Missing information should remain visible rather than be fabricated.

questions.stem: Why is a search-result snippet not usually enough for a research claim?
choices: It always contains the whole source.
It guarantees the source’s accuracy.
It replaces the need to identify an author.
It may omit the source’s context, methods, or qualifications.
questions.explanation: A snippet can help locate a source but is not a complete evaluation of it.

questions.stem: Which question can R2 address directly?
choices: How late closing finished on each trial date
Exactly how many unique visitors attended
Every visitor’s reason for coming
What all residents preferred
questions.explanation: R2 records closing times and procedural changes, not all visitor information.

questions.stem: Which actions belong in a research plan? Select all that apply.
choices: Match subquestions with relevant sources.
Decide the result before reading.
Record important information the sources do not provide.
Collect unrelated facts because they sound impressive.
questions.explanation: Planning keeps the inquiry focused and makes evidence gaps visible.

questions.stem: What term names a source that directly records an event being studied?
questions.explanation: A primary source supplies direct evidence relevant to the inquiry.

questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning in this lesson.
choices: A focused question directing an inquiry toward information
Direct evidence from the event or material being studied
A source interpreting or discussing other evidence
How well a source fits the information question
questions.explanation: research question: A focused question directing an inquiry toward information; primary source: Direct evidence from the event or material being studied; secondary source: A source interpreting or discussing other evidence; source relevance: How well a source fits the information question.

questions.stem: R3 asks about convenience. Which paraphrase preserves the measurement?
choices: Every resident prefers Thursday permanently.
All visitors became expert builders.
Seven of ten respondents called the hour convenient.
Everyone learned more than ever.
questions.explanation: “Seven of ten respondents called the hour convenient” preserves both the respondent group and the convenience measurement.

questions.stem: If you copy exact wording into notes, what should you do immediately?
choices: Remove every source label.
Change one adjective and call it entirely original.
Wait until you forget where it came from.
Mark it as a quotation and record its source.
questions.explanation: Immediate labeling prevents copied wording from being mistaken for your own later.

questions.stem: Does paraphrasing a borrowed idea remove the need for a citation?
choices: No; the idea still comes from the source.
Yes; any changed word removes attribution.
Yes; only books require citations.
No; therefore paraphrasing is forbidden.
questions.explanation: Attribution applies to borrowed ideas as well as exact wording.

questions.stem: A fictional packet document has no date. What should the reference say?
choices: A date from an unrelated source
No date supplied
An invented date chosen to look complete
The current date as if it were publication
questions.explanation: Missing information should be identified honestly.

questions.stem: Which practice distinguishes your analysis from source content?
choices: Attribute your new conclusion to the source automatically.
Remove quotation marks from copied sentences.
Label a note My thinking and keep it separate from quoted words.
Mix every sentence without labels.
questions.explanation: Clear labels preserve the origin and status of each note.

questions.stem: Why is an invented URL for a fictional packet source inappropriate?
choices: Every citation requires an invented link.
Fictional teaching packets cannot be identified.
URLs never help locate real sources.
It falsely suggests a real retrievable publication.
questions.explanation: The packet should be identified honestly as course material, without false external provenance.

questions.stem: R3 has 7 convenient, 2 inconvenient, and 1 blank response. How many total respondents are reported?
questions.explanation: The one blank answer remains part of the 10-person respondent total.

questions.stem: What is wrong with copying a source sentence and changing only two adjectives without quotation marks?
choices: A title automatically replaces quotation marks.
The source’s expression remains largely borrowed and is not clearly marked.
All ideas become new after two word changes.
Only numbers can be plagiarized.
questions.explanation: Minor substitutions do not make copied expression a genuinely new paraphrase.

questions.stem: Which actions make source use traceable? Select all that apply.
choices: Invent missing publication information.
Record author, title, date if supplied, and location.
Attribute flyer claims to records that do not support them.
Mark copied wording as quotation.
questions.explanation: Traceability depends on accurate source information and clear treatment of borrowed words.

questions.stem: What term names identification of a borrowed idea’s source?
questions.explanation: A citation identifies where borrowed information comes from.

questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning in this lesson.
choices: An accurate restatement of a source’s idea in new wording and structure
Identification of the source of borrowed information
Presenting another’s words or ideas as one’s own without appropriate acknowledgment
A record connecting information with the source needed to locate it
questions.explanation: paraphrase: An accurate restatement of a source’s idea in new wording and structure; citation: Identification of the source of borrowed information; plagiarism: Presenting another’s words or ideas as one’s own without appropriate acknowledgment; source note: A record connecting information with the source needed to locate it.

questions.stem: What does an evidence matrix organize?
choices: Only authors’ favorite colors
A poem’s rhyme sounds only
Unrelated quotations without labels
Source notes across subtopics or questions
questions.explanation: A matrix helps compare evidence and gaps by idea.

questions.stem: R1 counts 8, 11, 10, and 13 visits. What is the total?
choices: 42 visits
42 different people guaranteed
20 visits
84 visits
questions.explanation: The sum is 42, and the unit remains visits.

questions.stem: Which claim contradicts the sequence 8, 11, 10, 13?
choices: The four counts totaled 42 visits.
Attendance doubled every week.
Week 3 was lower than week 2.
Week 4 was higher than week 1.
questions.explanation: Weekly doubling does not match any complete pattern in these values.

questions.stem: Which organization best fits an explanation of use, operations, and unanswered questions?
choices: Only a paragraph about source titles
All evidence omitted until the last word
Sections grouped by those subtopics with relevant sources combined
A random list of quotations
questions.explanation: Topic-based organization makes relationships among sources visible.

questions.stem: Why distinguish 42 visits from 10 questionnaire respondents?
choices: They must be the same individuals.
Every visit includes a questionnaire by definition.
Numbers from one project can always be merged.
They are different measures from different collection scopes.
questions.explanation: The counts concern visits across four dates and responses at one session.

questions.stem: Which sentence attributes a questionable statement rather than adopting it?
choices: The flyer claims weekly doubling, but R1’s counts do not show it.
Attendance doubled because the flyer says so.
Every resident agrees, without any source.
No source has a perspective.
questions.explanation: The sentence identifies the claim’s origin and tests it against evidence.

questions.stem: R2 reports improved closing times after several changes. What remains uncertain?
choices: Whether week 1 was recorded as late
Which change caused the improvement
Whether the notes list closing times
Whether four trial dates are discussed
questions.explanation: The record does not isolate causes among the procedural changes.

questions.stem: Which thesis accurately frames the packet?
choices: The flyer replaces every record.
No information exists in the packet.
The records show use and operational changes but leave important questions unresolved.
The packet proves permanent success for every library.
questions.explanation: The bounded thesis accounts for both findings and limitations.

questions.stem: Which practices support synthesis? Select all that apply.
choices: Group sources around shared questions.
Explain both connections and limits.
Add unlike counts as if they measure the same population.
Repeat promotional claims without checking records.
questions.explanation: Synthesis connects relevant evidence while retaining distinctions and limits.

questions.stem: What term names language identifying who made a claim?
questions.explanation: Attribution makes the origin of a statement clear.

questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning in this lesson.
choices: The central explanation developed by an informational piece
A focused part of a larger subject or explanation
A table organizing source notes across questions or ideas
Language identifying who supplied information or made a claim
questions.explanation: informational thesis: The central explanation developed by an informational piece; subtopic: A focused part of a larger subject or explanation; evidence matrix: A table organizing source notes across questions or ideas; attribution: Language identifying who supplied information or made a claim.

questions.stem: A draft says 42 different people attended, but R1 counts visits. What correction is needed?
choices: Replace different people with visits and state that unique attendance is unknown.
Keep the phrase because it sounds stronger.
Double the number without evidence.
Delete the source definition.
questions.explanation: The unit must match the record; repeat visits may occur.

questions.stem: R2 records several procedural changes without isolating their effects. Which sentence is accurate?
choices: Every future event will close on time.
Delays decreased while the procedures changed; the notes do not isolate a cause.
The checklist alone caused every improvement.
The role assignments had no possible effect.
questions.explanation: The record supports a sequence and association, not an isolated causal conclusion.

questions.stem: What should happen if an accuracy correction changes a central result?
choices: Hide the correction in an unrelated footnote.
Assume grammar fixes everything.
Revisit the thesis and related conclusions.
Leave the thesis unchanged regardless of meaning.
questions.explanation: A changed result can affect the explanation built on it.

questions.stem: Which reference belongs in the final list?
choices: An impressive source never consulted
A fabricated publication
An invented link to a nonexistent document
A source actually used and accurately identified
questions.explanation: References document actual source use.

questions.stem: Why check a quotation for a missing not?
choices: Its omission can reverse the meaning.
Not is never meaningful.
Shorter quotations are always more accurate.
Quotation marks make every wording exact.
questions.explanation: Small words can change the direction of a source’s claim.

questions.stem: Does completing this research task require public internet posting?
choices: No; therefore the writing cannot be shared with a teacher.
No; submission within the learning setting is sufficient.
Yes; private drafts never count.
Yes; every personal detail must be published.
questions.explanation: The learning task can be completed without public disclosure.

questions.stem: Which question best checks reference usefulness?
choices: Are the authors’ names all the same length?
Can missing information be invented neatly?
Can another reader locate the source I used?
Does the list contain the largest possible number of titles?
questions.explanation: Traceability is the purpose of source identification.

questions.stem: What should a writer do with an impressive sentence that lacks support?
choices: Keep it because style outranks accuracy.
Add an unrelated citation.
Claim it came from every source.
Revise, qualify, support, or remove it.
questions.explanation: The sentence must fit the evidence or be changed.

questions.stem: Which checks belong in a source audit? Select all that apply.
choices: Add references never consulted.
Treat attractive formatting as proof of truth.
Verify numerical units against the source.
Compare quoted wording with the original.
questions.explanation: A source audit checks traceability and fidelity, not appearance or list length.

questions.stem: What term names the list identifying sources used in a piece?
questions.explanation: A reference list, bibliography, or works-cited list identifies sources according to the chosen convention.

questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning in this lesson.
choices: A check that borrowed information is accurately traceable to its sources
A repair to a statement that does not match the evidence
A list identifying the sources used in a piece
A decision about the audience and form for sharing work
questions.explanation: source audit: A check that borrowed information is accurately traceable to its sources; factual correction: A repair to a statement that does not match the evidence; reference list: A list identifying the sources used in a piece; publication choice: A decision about the audience and form for sharing work.

questions.stem: Which is an independent clause?
choices: When the recorder stopped
The recorder stopped.
Because the recorder stopped
Although the recorder stopped
questions.explanation: “The recorder stopped” can stand as a complete sentence without a dependent marker.

questions.stem: Which completes “When the last visitor left” as a formal sentence?
choices: When the last visitor left; although.
When the last visitor left, and because.
When the last visitor left, the volunteers counted the cards.
When the last visitor left, because the room.
questions.explanation: The complete main clause supplies the statement the dependent clause needs.

questions.stem: Which repair correctly joins two independent clauses?
choices: Arun pressed Play nothing happened.
Arun pressed Play, nothing happened.
Because Arun pressed Play; nothing happened.
Arun pressed Play, but nothing happened.
questions.explanation: A comma with the coordinating conjunction but joins the two independent clauses here.

questions.stem: What relationship does although usually introduce?
choices: Contrast with an expectation
A guaranteed cause
An alphabetical order
A source citation
questions.explanation: Although marks a contrast or concession rather than simply a result.

questions.stem: Why check meaning after combining sentences?
choices: Combining removes the need to read.
A connector can add a relationship the original evidence did not establish.
Grammar makes all evidence automatically correct.
Longer sentences always preserve every meaning.
questions.explanation: Words such as because and therefore can introduce unsupported causal claims.

questions.stem: Which sentence is complex?
choices: Inez saved the file, and Arun checked it.
Inez saved and checked the file.
After the call ended, Inez saved the file.
Inez saved the file.
questions.explanation: After the call ended is dependent, and Inez saved the file is independent.

questions.stem: What is a useful purpose of a short sentence in a paragraph?
choices: Proving that all long sentences are wrong
Replacing every explanation
Making every paragraph identical
Emphasizing an important point or turning moment
questions.explanation: Sentence length can guide attention when chosen for a purpose.

questions.stem: Which change overstates the evidence “They used a checklist and closed on time”?
choices: The checklist alone guarantees no future delay.
They followed the checklist and closed on time.
The volunteers used a checklist.
Closing finished at the planned time.
questions.explanation: A single observed sequence does not prove a sole cause or future guarantee.

questions.stem: Which practices improve sentence combining? Select all that apply.
choices: Choose a connector that fits the actual relationship.
Use therefore between any two nearby facts.
Join all complete clauses with commas alone.
Reread the revised sentence for preserved meaning.
questions.explanation: Meaning and correct clause connections matter more than length.

questions.stem: What term names a clause that can stand as a complete sentence?
questions.explanation: An independent or main clause can stand alone.

questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning in this lesson.
choices: A subject-and-verb unit that can stand as a complete sentence
A subject-and-verb unit that cannot stand alone in ordinary formal prose
A sentence joining independent clauses
A sentence combining an independent clause with a dependent clause
questions.explanation: independent clause: A subject-and-verb unit that can stand as a complete sentence; dependent clause: A subject-and-verb unit that cannot stand alone in ordinary formal prose; compound sentence: A sentence joining independent clauses; complex sentence: A sentence combining an independent clause with a dependent clause.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses formal subject case correctly?
choices: Me tested the recorder with Arun.
Him and me tested the recorder.
Arun and I tested the recorder.
Arun and me tested the recorder.
questions.explanation: I is part of the subject, so subject case fits.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses object case correctly after to?
choices: Give the list to Arun and I.
Give the list to he and I.
Give the list to we.
Give the list to Arun and me.
questions.explanation: Me is an object of the preposition to.

questions.stem: What is the job of herself in “Inez herself checked the file”?
choices: Intensive emphasis
A replacement for every object pronoun
A possessive before a noun
A dialogue tag
questions.explanation: Removing herself leaves the basic sentence complete; it emphasizes who checked.

questions.stem: Which revision makes Asha the person holding the key?
choices: Maya had the key, not Asha.
Maya said that Asha had the key.
Maya told Asha that she had it.
She told her that she had it.
questions.explanation: Repeating Asha’s name establishes the intended reference.

questions.stem: Which possessive pronoun correctly completes “The volunteers own this list; it is ___”?
choices: they
themselves
theirs
them
questions.explanation: Theirs indicates belonging without requiring another noun.

questions.stem: Is singular they automatically an error in “A visitor may leave their question”?
choices: Yes; it can never refer to one person.
Yes; the visitor must be assigned a gender.
No; therefore every unclear pronoun is acceptable.
No; it can clearly refer to an unspecified visitor.
questions.explanation: Singular they can be inclusive and clear; reference still needs to be understandable.

questions.stem: Why can “Maya spoke to Asha, and she sounded worried” be unclear?
choices: She could refer to either person without more context.
Every sentence with a pronoun is wrong.
The pronoun must always mean the nearest name.
The sentence contains no people.
questions.explanation: Two plausible antecedents create ambiguity.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses herself as an object referring back to the subject?
choices: Inez, herself, performed the check.
Inez taught herself to use the recorder.
Inez herself checked the recorder.
Inez checked the recorder herself.
questions.explanation: In taught herself, the pronoun identifies who received the teaching.

questions.stem: Which editing choices improve pronoun use? Select all that apply.
choices: Always choose I because it sounds formal.
Choose case by the pronoun’s role.
Repeat a name when needed to clarify reference.
Assume a pronoun must refer to the nearest noun regardless of context.
questions.explanation: Role and clear reference guide effective pronoun choices.

questions.stem: Complete the formal sentence with I or me: “The librarian thanked Arun and ___.”
questions.explanation: The pronoun is part of the object of thanked, so me fits.

questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning in this lesson.
choices: A pronoun functioning as a sentence subject
A pronoun functioning as an object of a verb or preposition
A pronoun indicating belonging, such as mine or theirs
A pronoun form such as herself used to add removable emphasis
questions.explanation: subject pronoun: A pronoun functioning as a sentence subject; object pronoun: A pronoun functioning as an object of a verb or preposition; possessive pronoun: A pronoun indicating belonging, such as mine or theirs; intensive pronoun: A pronoun form such as herself used to add removable emphasis.

questions.stem: In “My only brother, Leo, helped,” why is Leo set off with commas?
choices: Every proper name always needs commas.
The sentence has more than one brother.
Commas mark every subject.
The name adds information to an already identified person.
questions.explanation: Only brother already identifies the person; the name is added information.

questions.stem: “The students who finished stayed” identifies a subset. Should commas automatically surround who finished?
choices: No; the clause identifies which students.
Yes; every who clause is nonrestrictive.
Yes; the clause has a verb.
No; commas are never used in sentences.
questions.explanation: The identifying function makes the clause restrictive in this context.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses all three forms correctly?
choices: They’re putting there model over their.
They’re putting their model over there.
Their putting there model over they’re.
There putting they’re model over their.
questions.explanation: They’re means they are, their shows belonging, and there indicates place.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses its?
choices: Its been checked twice.
Its a useful model.
The model lost its label.
Its ready to display.
questions.explanation: Its is the possessive form; the other sentences need it’s.

questions.stem: Which sentence keeps two yesterday actions in past tense?
choices: Yesterday, Inez tests the recorder and saved the file.
Yesterday, Inez tested the recorder and saves the file.
Yesterday, Inez testing the recorder and saves the file.
Yesterday, Inez tested the recorder and saved the file.
questions.explanation: Tested and saved consistently place both actions in the past.

questions.stem: Which punctuation can set off an aside?
choices: Paired parentheses around the aside
An unmatched opening parenthesis only
A comma replacing every verb
A question mark in the middle of every noun
questions.explanation: Parentheses can enclose added information while the main sentence continues.

questions.stem: Why might a spellchecker miss a wrong use of their?
choices: Punctuation makes spelling irrelevant.
Their is a real word even when the sentence needs another form.
Spellcheckers prove every sentence’s meaning.
Their is never a real word.
questions.explanation: Correct spelling does not establish the correct word for the intended meaning.

questions.stem: Which form simply means more than one model?
choices: models’s
model is
models
model’s
questions.explanation: The regular plural models does not require an apostrophe.

questions.stem: Which checks belong in convention editing? Select all that apply.
choices: Determine whether a clause identifies or adds information.
Put commas around every proper name.
Choose homophones according to intended meaning.
Add apostrophes to all plural nouns.
questions.explanation: Convention choices depend on grammatical function and meaning, not mechanical additions.

questions.stem: Complete with its or it’s: “The bridge model needs ___ own label.”
questions.explanation: Its is the possessive form meaning belonging to it.

questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning in this lesson.
choices: Added information not needed to identify the person or thing
Information needed to identify which person or thing is meant
An aside or interruption within a sentence
A word pronounced like another word but differing in meaning or spelling
questions.explanation: nonrestrictive element: Added information not needed to identify the person or thing; restrictive element: Information needed to identify which person or thing is meant; parenthetical element: An aside or interruption within a sentence; homophone: A word pronounced like another word but differing in meaning or spelling.

questions.stem: Which request is precise and appropriate for a reviewer unfamiliar with the project?
choices: Please check whether my final paragraph’s conclusion follows from the data.
Check the thing because stuff is weird.
Undertake all conceivable evaluative operations immediately.
You must praise everything without reading.
questions.explanation: Asking whether the final paragraph’s conclusion follows from the data identifies a precise review task respectfully.

questions.stem: What is register?
choices: A rule that every word must be long
Language choices suited to a situation and audience
A measure of a speaker’s worth
The number of pages in a book
questions.explanation: Register concerns context and communicative choices.

questions.stem: Which revision is most precise?
choices: It was good in every way.
Stuff improved somehow.
The labeled tray helped visitors find blank cards.
The thing made everything better.
questions.explanation: The precise sentence identifies the object, action, and specific benefit.

questions.stem: What is redundant in “The final ending concluded at the very end”?
choices: The sentence contains a verb.
The sentence has a capital letter.
Every sentence about endings is forbidden.
Several phrases repeat the idea of ending without adding meaning.
questions.explanation: The repeated generality can be replaced with a specific observation.

questions.stem: Which statement treats language variation respectfully?
choices: Different settings call for different language choices; dialect does not measure intelligence.
Every informal speaker is unintelligent.
Only one community has meaningful language.
Formal language must replace all family speech.
questions.explanation: Learning additional registers expands choices without ranking people’s worth.

questions.stem: Which sentence reports an action without inventing a hostile motive?
choices: The coordinator never cares about anyone.
The coordinator requested a staffing plan before approval.
The coordinator hates every visitor.
The coordinator blocked the plan because of secret malice.
questions.explanation: The stated action is supported without guessing a motive.

questions.stem: Should every repeated word be removed?
choices: Yes; clarity never benefits from repeated terms.
No; therefore all repetition is useful.
No; repetition can serve a deliberate purpose.
Yes; poems cannot repeat sounds or words.
questions.explanation: Repetition can aid cohesion or emphasis; redundancy is repetition without useful work.

questions.stem: Which question best guides style revision?
choices: How can every word become longer?
How can I hide the main action?
How can I make the source sound more certain than it is?
What helps this audience understand this purpose?
questions.explanation: Style should serve communication rather than complexity for its own sake.

questions.stem: Which choices can improve style? Select all that apply.
choices: Treat all dialects except one as evidence of low intelligence.
Replace vague wording with a specific supported statement.
Use the longest available word regardless of clarity.
Match the request’s register to its audience.
questions.explanation: Precision and audience fit improve communication without disrespecting language variation.

questions.stem: What term names the attitude conveyed by wording?
questions.explanation: Tone is the attitude communicated through language and presentation.

questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning in this lesson.
choices: The kind and level of language suited to a situation and audience
The attitude conveyed through wording and presentation
Exactness in expressing an intended meaning
Unnecessary repetition that adds no useful meaning
questions.explanation: register: The kind and level of language suited to a situation and audience; tone: The attitude conveyed through wording and presentation; precision: Exactness in expressing an intended meaning; redundancy: Unnecessary repetition that adds no useful meaning.

questions.stem: Which preparation best supports a discussion about a story?
choices: A prediction of who will win
A question, two text locations, and one uncertainty
A speech that cannot change
Only a list of people you agree with
questions.explanation: Evidence and an open question prepare a learner to contribute and reconsider.

questions.stem: Which response checks understanding?
choices: There is nothing left to discuss.
Your idea is impossible because it is yours.
Do you mean that embarrassment explains the hidden card?
You must agree with me now.
questions.explanation: Asking “Do you mean that embarrassment explains the hidden card?” offers a restatement for confirmation or correction.

questions.stem: Which question develops a claim about Maya’s embarrassment?
choices: What is your favorite lunch?
Can I speak for the rest of the time?
Why are all your answers wrong?
How does turning the card face down support that idea?
questions.explanation: The question asks for a reasoning connection to relevant evidence.

questions.stem: What should a listener do when new evidence weakens an earlier interpretation?
choices: Reconsider the interpretation and explain the change
Ignore the evidence to avoid changing
Accuse the source of being unfair without reading it
Pretend the new evidence was never offered
questions.explanation: Discussion can improve an interpretation through revision.

questions.stem: Which is respectful disagreement?
choices: Your view has no value because it differs.
I read the final line differently because Eli also takes a card.
Only a foolish person would think that.
Stop speaking so I can win.
questions.explanation: The response challenges an interpretation through textual evidence.

questions.stem: Why should a recorder note unresolved questions?
choices: They replace every piece of evidence
They guarantee that no answer exists
They identify what the group still needs to investigate
They prove the group learned nothing
questions.explanation: An unresolved question can define a useful next step.

questions.stem: What does a solo simulated discussion demonstrate most directly?
choices: Verified listening to a real partner
Agreement from classmates who were absent
A recording of an actual group
Preparation and construction of possible responses
questions.explanation: A simulation is preparation; its evidence should not be mislabeled as live interaction.

questions.stem: Which participation practice is useful?
choices: Allow thinking time and written contributions
Require identical speaking speed from everyone
Treat silence as automatic agreement
Let the facilitator make every claim
questions.explanation: Different participation methods can support a shared inquiry.

questions.stem: Which actions support active listening? Select all that apply.
choices: Restate an idea and invite correction.
Connect a follow-up question to the speaker’s evidence.
Prepare an unrelated speech while ignoring the speaker.
Assume that being quiet means agreeing.
questions.explanation: Listening attends to meaning and checks it rather than making assumptions.

questions.stem: What term from this lesson names an agreed expectation for participation?
questions.explanation: A discussion norm is an agreed expectation.

questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning in this lesson.
choices: An agreed expectation that supports a shared conversation
Attending to another person’s meaning and responding to it
A question that develops something already said
A restatement offered to check understanding of another person’s idea
questions.explanation: discussion norm: An agreed expectation that supports a shared conversation; active listening: Attending to another person’s meaning and responding to it; follow-up question: A question that develops something already said; paraphrase check: A restatement offered to check understanding of another person’s idea.

questions.stem: Which purpose is manageable for a short presentation?
choices: Mention every possible topic without a focus
Read a list of numbers without a question
Explain what the four-week trial can and cannot show
Tell everything ever written about libraries
questions.explanation: The focused purpose sets a feasible scope and invites evidence and limits.

questions.stem: Which statement accurately presents the R1 total?
choices: The record proves 42 different people attended.
Exactly 42 people learned more.
All residents attended each Thursday.
The record counts 42 visits over four Thursdays; repeat visits may be included.
questions.explanation: The source counts visits, not unique people or learning outcomes.

questions.stem: What does “Next, consider closing time” do?
choices: Signals a change to a new main point
Provides the entire evidence for a cause
Replaces the need for an introduction
Proves the previous speaker was wrong
questions.explanation: The phrase signposts the presentation’s organization.

questions.stem: A rehearsal reveals an overloaded sentence. What is a useful revision?
choices: Invent a shorter source result
Divide its ideas and add a transition and pause
Say it faster without changing anything
Remove all explanations but keep the numbers
questions.explanation: Clear spoken units help the audience follow the reasoning.

questions.stem: What should a speaker do after forgetting a source number?
choices: Change the topic and claim the number was proven
Assume every audience estimate is correct
Check the notes or acknowledge the gap
Invent a confident answer
questions.explanation: Accuracy matters more than pretending to remember.

questions.stem: Which visual description best supports access?
choices: The picture says everything.
You can see it, so I need not explain.
Ignore the labels and trust the tallest bar.
The four weekly counts are 8, 11, 10, and 13 visits, with a dip in week 3.
questions.explanation: The description communicates the important values and pattern.

questions.stem: What can an annotated transcript directly show?
choices: Planned wording, pauses, and source cues
Proof of every feature of a live delivery
Approval from an audience that never saw it
A recording that was never made
questions.explanation: A plan is useful evidence of planning but should not be mislabeled as observed performance.

questions.stem: Which conclusion fits an informative trial presentation?
choices: No evidence matters if the speaker feels confident.
The records describe use and closing, while learning outcomes remain unknown.
Everyone learned more because the room was open.
The first number proves every future trial will succeed.
questions.explanation: The conclusion synthesizes findings and preserves the limits.

questions.stem: Which actions improve an evidence-based presentation? Select all that apply.
choices: Use volume as a replacement for evidence.
Treat a script as proof that a live audience understood.
Identify the source and unit of an important number.
Rehearse and revise a place where the logic is hard to follow.
questions.explanation: Accurate evidence and deliberate revision improve trust and clarity.

questions.stem: What term names purposeful practice before presenting?
questions.explanation: Rehearsal reveals changes needed in content and delivery.

questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning in this lesson.
choices: A plan of major points and their supporting details
The background, explanations, and access supports an audience needs
Words or phrases that show the direction of a presentation
Purposeful practice used to improve content and delivery
questions.explanation: presentation outline: A plan of major points and their supporting details; audience needs: The background, explanations, and access supports an audience needs; signposting: Words or phrases that show the direction of a presentation; rehearsal: Purposeful practice used to improve content and delivery.

questions.stem: Which pair of weekly counts contradicts “attendance rose every week”?
choices: Week 1 had 8 and week 2 had 11
Week 3 had 10 and week 4 had 13
Week 1 had 8 and week 4 had 13
Week 2 had 11 and week 3 had 10
questions.explanation: The decrease from 11 to 10 contradicts an increase in every consecutive week.

questions.stem: Which finding is supported by Slide A?
choices: The final weekly count is higher than the first.
Every week had more visits than the previous week.
Every visitor learned more.
Each visit was made by a different person.
questions.explanation: Thirteen is greater than eight; the other claims require missing or conflicting evidence.

questions.stem: Why does Slide B not represent all residents?
choices: The blank response proves all absent people agree
It reports voluntary respondents at one final session
It contains more than one category
A table can never show evidence
questions.explanation: The selection of respondents limits the population represented.

questions.stem: What should happen to the blank response in a report of all ten respondents?
choices: Count it as convenient without evidence
Count it as inconvenient without evidence
Keep it as a reported category
Delete it and still claim the total is ten answered items
questions.explanation: Blank is part of the reported total and does not establish either preference.

questions.stem: Why use a zero baseline for a simple bar chart of these visits?
choices: So the data prove a cause
So labels become unnecessary
So every bar has the same height
So bar lengths represent the values proportionally
questions.explanation: Beginning at zero avoids exaggerating value ratios through truncated bar lengths.

questions.stem: What kind of relationship do Slide B’s rows show?
choices: Different response categories from one questionnaire
Three consecutive weeks of declining opinions
The ages of all residents
A measurement of learning across four lessons
questions.explanation: The row labels name categories, not time periods.

questions.stem: Which is an accessible description of Slide A?
choices: The right bar looks nice.
Visits were 8, 11, 10, and 13, with a decrease between weeks 2 and 3.
The blue shape goes there.
Everything important is in the picture.
questions.explanation: The description gives values and pattern without relying on color or position.

questions.stem: Which additional evidence would be needed to examine learning gains?
choices: A more confident reading of the same unsupported claim
A larger title for the attendance table
An appropriate measure of learning, beyond attendance and convenience
A brighter slide background
questions.explanation: The existing records do not measure learning outcomes.

questions.stem: Which checks help compare speech and a visual? Select all that apply.
choices: Test each spoken assertion against the displayed values.
Treat confident delivery as proof.
Assume response categories are consecutive dates.
Read the units, source, labels, and time period.
questions.explanation: Checking claims and labels keeps the interpretation tied to the evidence.

questions.stem: What word names the relationship between chart marks and represented values?
questions.explanation: A scale connects chart positions or marks with values.

questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning in this lesson.
choices: A table, chart, diagram, or other visual organization of information
The relationship between marks or positions on a chart and represented values
A statement of important visual information that does not require seeing the image
An assertion made in speech that can be examined for evidence
questions.explanation: visual display: A table, chart, diagram, or other visual organization of information; scale: The relationship between marks or positions on a chart and represented values; accessible description: A statement of important visual information that does not require seeing the image; spoken claim: An assertion made in speech that can be examined for evidence.

questions.topic: A portfolio of growth and revision
questions.stem: What makes a collection a purposeful portfolio?
choices: Selections are labeled and explained as evidence of learning
It contains every file without explanation
It hides all earlier versions
It claims every skill is perfect
questions.explanation: A portfolio connects selected work to learning and reflection.

questions.topic: A portfolio of growth and revision
questions.stem: Which is useful revision evidence?
choices: An unrelated decoration
An earlier claim, its revised version, and an explanation of the improved scope
Only the statement “I tried hard”
A missing draft and an invented quotation from it
questions.explanation: Before-and-after evidence makes the change visible and explainable.

questions.topic: A portfolio of growth and revision
questions.stem: Which goal is specific enough to guide practice?
choices: Never have any difficulty again.
Finish without rereading.
In my next two responses, connect each quotation to its claim with an explanation.
Be better at everything.
questions.explanation: The goal identifies a skill, action, and practice opportunity.

questions.topic: A portfolio of growth and revision
questions.stem: What should a learner do if a later piece is weaker in one way?
choices: Hide the piece and invent a stronger result
Claim growth must be identical in every skill
Ignore all criteria forever
Identify the weakness and make a supported revision plan
questions.explanation: Honest reflection can use an uneven result to guide improvement.

questions.topic: A portfolio of growth and revision
questions.stem: What does a quiz score alone fail to establish?
choices: The quality of an original story and an unobserved discussion
Which bounded quiz items were answered correctly
That the quiz was attempted if the record shows it
The recorded numerical quiz result
questions.explanation: Open writing and live communication require different evidence from a bounded quiz.

questions.topic: A portfolio of growth and revision
questions.stem: Which portfolio label is accurate for a solo imagined conversation?
choices: Teacher-approved performance when no teacher reviewed it
Simulated exchange showing preparation
Verified group discussion with classmates
Recorded live listening assessment
questions.explanation: The label should identify the activity actually completed.

questions.topic: A portfolio of growth and revision
questions.stem: How can a learner support a rubric self-rating?
choices: Assume spelling alone measures every criterion
Invent a reviewer’s comment
Point to a specific place in the work that matches the criterion
Repeat the score without evidence
questions.explanation: Criteria become useful when linked to observable features of the work.

questions.topic: A portfolio of growth and revision
questions.stem: Which reflection is most useful?
choices: Everything is perfect because I finished.
Nothing can improve because I made one error.
My files are numerous, so the reasoning must be correct.
I narrowed my claim to the sampled respondents; next I will explain quotation connections more clearly.
questions.explanation: The reflection identifies a concrete improvement and a next learning need.

questions.topic: A portfolio of growth and revision
questions.stem: Which belong in an honest growth portfolio? Select all that apply.
choices: A fabricated teacher approval.
A meaningful before-and-after revision with explanation.
Goals connected to evidence in selected work.
A claim that a planned performance was observed.
questions.explanation: Visible revision and evidence-based goals show learning without inventing feedback or performance.

questions.topic: A portfolio of growth and revision
questions.stem: What term names a purposeful collection of learning work?
questions.explanation: A portfolio gathers selected work to show learning.

questions.topic: A portfolio of growth and revision
questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning in this lesson.
choices: A purposeful collection of work showing learning
An explanation of learning, its evidence, and a next step
An earlier and changed version paired with an explanation
A skill to improve through a specific next action
questions.explanation: portfolio: A purposeful collection of work showing learning; reflection: An explanation of learning, its evidence, and a next step; revision evidence: An earlier and changed version paired with an explanation; learning goal: A skill to improve through a specific next action.

cards.front: textual evidence — what does it mean?
cards.back: A detail from a text used to support an idea about it

cards.front: explicit detail — what does it mean?
cards.back: Information directly stated in the text

cards.front: quotation — what does it mean?
cards.back: The exact words of a source, marked as borrowed words

cards.front: location reference — what does it mean?
cards.back: Information that helps a reader find a detail in a source

cards.front: Apply it: Evidence and quotations
cards.back: State an answer, choose a relevant detail, locate it, and explain how it supports your answer.

cards.front: inference — what does it mean?
cards.back: A conclusion supported by clues and reasonable thinking

cards.front: clue — what does it mean?
cards.back: A detail that helps a reader reach a conclusion

cards.front: counterevidence — what does it mean?
cards.back: A detail that challenges a proposed conclusion

cards.front: strength of support — what does it mean?
cards.back: How closely and consistently evidence fits a conclusion

cards.front: Apply it: Making supported inferences
cards.back: Collect clues, explain the connection, test an alternative, and limit your certainty to what the evidence supports.

cards.front: summary — what does it mean?
cards.back: A shortened account of a text’s main ideas or important events

cards.front: objective summary — what does it mean?
cards.back: A summary that keeps personal judgment separate from source content

cards.front: major event — what does it mean?
cards.back: An event that changes the main situation or explains an important decision

cards.front: sequence — what does it mean?
cards.back: The order in which events or steps occur

cards.front: Apply it: Summarizing without judging
cards.back: Identify the central situation, select important developments, preserve their connections, and remove unsupported judgment.

cards.front: context — what does it mean?
cards.back: The surrounding language and situation that help establish meaning

cards.front: prefix — what does it mean?
cards.back: A meaningful word part added at the beginning of a base

cards.front: suffix — what does it mean?
cards.back: A meaningful word part added at the end of a base

cards.front: reference entry — what does it mean?
cards.back: Information about a word, including meanings and often usage examples

cards.front: Apply it: Vocabulary in context
cards.back: Read around the word, propose a meaning, test it in the sentence, and verify the appropriate sense when needed.

cards.front: setting — what does it mean?
cards.back: The time, place, and surrounding conditions of a story

cards.front: plot — what does it mean?
cards.back: The organized sequence of story events and their connections

cards.front: conflict — what does it mean?
cards.back: A struggle involving obstacles or incompatible goals

cards.front: motivation — what does it mean?
cards.back: A desire, reason, or pressure that drives a character’s action

cards.front: Apply it: Plot, setting, and conflict
cards.back: Track each important event by asking what changed, what the character wants, and what choice follows.

cards.front: characterization — what does it mean?
cards.back: How a text develops a character through details such as actions and speech

cards.front: trait — what does it mean?
cards.back: A relatively lasting quality suggested by a pattern of behavior

cards.front: emotion — what does it mean?
cards.back: A feeling experienced in a particular situation

cards.front: development — what does it mean?
cards.back: A meaningful change or deepening across a text

cards.front: Apply it: Character choices and change
cards.back: Compare a character’s self-description with several actions, then explain both the pattern and its limits.

cards.front: narrator — what does it mean?
cards.back: The voice that tells a story

cards.front: point of view — what does it mean?
cards.back: The position from which events are presented

cards.front: first-person narrator — what does it mean?
cards.back: A storyteller who participates using I or we

cards.front: third-person narrator — what does it mean?
cards.back: A storyteller who refers to characters using names or third-person pronouns

cards.front: Apply it: Narrator and point of view
cards.back: Separate dialogue from narration, ask whose knowledge is available, and explain what that access lets readers understand.

cards.front: theme — what does it mean?
cards.back: A larger idea about experience developed by a literary work

cards.front: topic — what does it mean?
cards.back: A subject a text explores

cards.front: theme statement — what does it mean?
cards.back: A complete sentence expressing a testable interpretation of a larger idea

cards.front: synthesis — what does it mean?
cards.back: A connected understanding formed by bringing evidence or ideas together

cards.front: Apply it: Theme across a whole novel
cards.back: Propose a larger idea, test it across the whole work, account for the ending, and revise overbroad claims.

cards.front: central idea — what does it mean?
cards.back: The main point developed across an informational passage

cards.front: supporting detail — what does it mean?
cards.back: A detail that explains, illustrates, or establishes a main point

cards.front: topic sentence — what does it mean?
cards.back: A sentence that states a paragraph’s main idea

cards.front: elaboration — what does it mean?
cards.back: Added explanation or examples that develop an idea

cards.front: Apply it: Central ideas and supporting details
cards.back: Propose a central idea, test it across the passage, and explain what each relevant detail contributes.

cards.front: text structure — what does it mean?
cards.back: The organization of ideas and their relationships

cards.front: chronological structure — what does it mean?
cards.back: Organization that follows time order

cards.front: cause-and-effect structure — what does it mean?
cards.back: Organization that explains how events contribute to outcomes

cards.front: problem-and-solution structure — what does it mean?
cards.back: Organization around a difficulty and a response

cards.front: Apply it: How text structure develops ideas
cards.back: Name the relationship between ideas and explain how that organization helps a reader understand the passage.

cards.front: purpose — what does it mean?
cards.back: What a text is trying to accomplish for its audience

cards.front: perspective — what does it mean?
cards.back: The position or outlook shaping a writer’s emphasis

cards.front: claim — what does it mean?
cards.back: A statement that can be supported or challenged

cards.front: credibility — what does it mean?
cards.back: How much trust a source deserves for a specific information need

cards.front: Apply it: Purpose, perspective, and claims
cards.back: Identify purpose, trace each claim to evidence, match expertise to the question, and state the limits.

cards.front: medium — what does it mean?
cards.back: The form used to communicate information

cards.front: representation — what does it mean?
cards.back: A particular way information is shown or described

cards.front: corroboration — what does it mean?
cards.back: Supporting evidence from sources for the same claim

cards.front: discrepancy — what does it mean?
cards.back: A difference between accounts or representations that needs explanation

cards.front: Apply it: Comparing texts and media
cards.back: Compare the same claim and unit across forms, explain each contribution, and investigate discrepancies before concluding.

cards.front: narrative — what does it mean?
cards.back: A text that presents connected events involving characters or a speaker

cards.front: orientation — what does it mean?
cards.back: Information that establishes the initial people, place, and situation

cards.front: turning point — what does it mean?
cards.back: An event or choice that redirects the action

cards.front: resolution — what does it mean?
cards.back: The result of the main struggle or the situation at the ending

cards.front: Apply it: Planning a meaningful narrative
cards.back: Narrow the event, identify a goal and obstacle, and connect a meaningful choice to its consequence.

cards.front: scene — what does it mean?
cards.back: A particular narrative moment developed through action and detail

cards.front: sensory detail — what does it mean?
cards.back: Description appealing to one or more senses

cards.front: dialogue — what does it mean?
cards.back: Spoken conversation represented in writing

cards.front: dialogue tag — what does it mean?
cards.back: Words identifying a speaker, such as she said or he asked

cards.front: Apply it: Scenes, description, and dialogue
cards.back: Choose a consequential moment, develop purposeful details, and make each exchange change what the characters know or do.

cards.front: pacing — what does it mean?
cards.back: The speed and emphasis with which a narrative presents events

cards.front: scene time — what does it mean?
cards.back: Narrative treatment that expands a particular moment

cards.front: narrative summary — what does it mean?
cards.back: A compressed account of a longer interval or less central events

cards.front: transition — what does it mean?
cards.back: Language connecting parts by time, place, or relationship

cards.front: Apply it: Pacing, transitions, and endings
cards.back: Expand the important choice, compress routine time, and check that transitions and the ending preserve clear consequences.

cards.front: revision — what does it mean?
cards.back: Changes to ideas, organization, development, or expression to improve a piece

cards.front: editing — what does it mean?
cards.back: Correction of conventions such as spelling and punctuation

cards.front: feedback — what does it mean?
cards.back: Information about a reader’s experience and possible improvements

cards.front: revision rationale — what does it mean?
cards.back: An explanation of why a change serves the writing’s purpose

cards.front: Apply it: Revising a narrative for readers
cards.back: Read for the central change, revise the largest meaning problem, use specific feedback, and then edit conventions.

cards.front: argument — what does it mean?
cards.back: Reasons and evidence used to support a position
cards.topic: A debatable claim and focused reasons

cards.front: debatable claim — what does it mean?
cards.back: A position that reasonable readers could question or dispute
cards.topic: A debatable claim and focused reasons

cards.front: reason — what does it mean?
cards.back: An explanation of why a position should be accepted
cards.topic: A debatable claim and focused reasons

cards.front: scope — what does it mean?
cards.back: The boundary of what a statement or inquiry covers
cards.topic: A debatable claim and focused reasons

cards.front: Apply it: A debatable claim and focused reasons
cards.back: Identify the actual decision, state a bounded position, and give distinct reasons that fit the available evidence.
cards.topic: A debatable claim and focused reasons

cards.front: relevant evidence — what does it mean?
cards.back: Evidence that directly bears on the claim under discussion

cards.front: reasoning — what does it mean?
cards.back: The explanation connecting evidence with a conclusion

cards.front: sufficient support — what does it mean?
cards.back: Enough appropriate evidence for a claim’s strength and scope

cards.front: qualification — what does it mean?
cards.back: A limit or condition that makes a statement fit what is known

cards.front: Apply it: Evidence and the reasoning bridge
cards.back: Use a relevant fact, explain why it matters, and check whether the resulting claim is stronger than the evidence.

cards.front: counterclaim — what does it mean?
cards.back: A position that challenges the writer’s claim

cards.front: concession — what does it mean?
cards.back: Acknowledgment of a valid point in another position

cards.front: response — what does it mean?
cards.back: An explanation addressing a challenge to an argument

cards.front: fair paraphrase — what does it mean?
cards.back: An accurate restatement of another idea in the writer’s own words

cards.front: Apply it: Considering another position fairly
cards.back: State the real concern fairly, acknowledge what is valid, and answer that concern with evidence or a concrete change.

cards.front: introduction — what does it mean?
cards.back: The opening that provides context and the direction of a piece

cards.front: cohesion — what does it mean?
cards.back: The connected flow among sentences and ideas

cards.front: conclusion — what does it mean?
cards.back: A purposeful ending that draws together the developed reasoning

cards.front: argument revision — what does it mean?
cards.back: Improving a position’s support, organization, clarity, and fairness

cards.front: Apply it: Drafting and revising an argument
cards.back: Check scope consistency, paragraph roles, evidence links, fair response, and a conclusion that does not outrun the support.

cards.front: imagery — what does it mean?
cards.back: Language that evokes sensory experience

cards.front: speaker — what does it mean?
cards.back: The voice presented in a poem

cards.front: alliteration — what does it mean?
cards.back: Repetition of an initial consonant sound in nearby words

cards.front: onomatopoeia — what does it mean?
cards.back: Use of words that suggest sounds

cards.front: Apply it: Imagery, sound, and the speaker
cards.back: Notice a specific image or sound, locate it, and explain its contribution to the poem’s situation or meaning.

cards.front: figurative language — what does it mean?
cards.back: Language extending beyond a literal sense for comparison or emphasis

cards.front: simile — what does it mean?
cards.back: An explicit comparison, often using like or as

cards.front: metaphor — what does it mean?
cards.back: A comparison presenting one thing in terms of another

cards.front: connotation — what does it mean?
cards.back: Associations or feelings a word can carry beyond its basic definition

cards.front: Apply it: Figurative language and word choice
cards.back: Identify the compared things, test the shared quality in context, and explain the effect of the particular wording.

cards.front: line break — what does it mean?
cards.back: The point where one line of verse ends and another begins

cards.front: stanza — what does it mean?
cards.back: A grouped set of lines in a poem

cards.front: rhyme — what does it mean?
cards.back: A correspondence of ending sounds

cards.front: free verse — what does it mean?
cards.back: Poetry without a fixed regular meter or rhyme scheme

cards.front: Apply it: Lines, stanzas, and poetic meaning
cards.back: Describe the actual line and stanza pattern, then connect its arrangement and sounds to the poem’s development.

cards.front: drama — what does it mean?
cards.back: A work designed for performance by speakers or actors

cards.front: stage direction — what does it mean?
cards.back: A script instruction describing action, setting, or delivery

cards.front: adaptation — what does it mean?
cards.back: A work reshaped for another form or purpose

cards.front: subtext — what does it mean?
cards.back: Unstated meaning or pressure suggested beneath spoken words

cards.front: Apply it: Drama and adapting a scene
cards.back: Separate speech from directions, infer subtext from evidence, and explain what performance or adaptation adds.

cards.front: research question — what does it mean?
cards.back: A focused question directing an inquiry toward information

cards.front: primary source — what does it mean?
cards.back: Direct evidence from the event or material being studied

cards.front: secondary source — what does it mean?
cards.back: A source interpreting or discussing other evidence

cards.front: source relevance — what does it mean?
cards.back: How well a source fits the information question

cards.front: Apply it: Focused questions and useful sources
cards.back: Narrow the question, separate it into subquestions, and match each to evidence while recording unresolved gaps.

cards.front: paraphrase — what does it mean?
cards.back: An accurate restatement of a source’s idea in new wording and structure

cards.front: citation — what does it mean?
cards.back: Identification of the source of borrowed information

cards.front: plagiarism — what does it mean?
cards.back: Presenting another’s words or ideas as one’s own without appropriate acknowledgment

cards.front: source note — what does it mean?
cards.back: A record connecting information with the source needed to locate it

cards.front: Apply it: Notes, paraphrases, and citations
cards.back: Keep exact words, paraphrases, and your thinking separate, and attach a traceable source reference to borrowed information.

cards.front: informational thesis — what does it mean?
cards.back: The central explanation developed by an informational piece

cards.front: subtopic — what does it mean?
cards.back: A focused part of a larger subject or explanation

cards.front: evidence matrix — what does it mean?
cards.back: A table organizing source notes across questions or ideas

cards.front: attribution — what does it mean?
cards.back: Language identifying who supplied information or made a claim

cards.front: Apply it: Organizing a researched explanation
cards.back: Organize by questions, combine relevant sources, preserve their units and limits, and explain how their information relates.

cards.front: source audit — what does it mean?
cards.back: A check that borrowed information is accurately traceable to its sources

cards.front: factual correction — what does it mean?
cards.back: A repair to a statement that does not match the evidence

cards.front: reference list — what does it mean?
cards.back: A list identifying the sources used in a piece

cards.front: publication choice — what does it mean?
cards.back: A decision about the audience and form for sharing work

cards.front: Apply it: Revising and sharing research
cards.back: Verify claims against sources, repair meaning errors, recheck organization, and share through a suitable learning format.

cards.front: independent clause — what does it mean?
cards.back: A subject-and-verb unit that can stand as a complete sentence

cards.front: dependent clause — what does it mean?
cards.back: A subject-and-verb unit that cannot stand alone in ordinary formal prose

cards.front: compound sentence — what does it mean?
cards.back: A sentence joining independent clauses

cards.front: complex sentence — what does it mean?
cards.back: A sentence combining an independent clause with a dependent clause

cards.front: Apply it: Sentences and meaningful combinations
cards.back: Find the complete clauses, choose the intended relationship, combine appropriately, and reread for meaning.

cards.front: subject pronoun — what does it mean?
cards.back: A pronoun functioning as a sentence subject

cards.front: object pronoun — what does it mean?
cards.back: A pronoun functioning as an object of a verb or preposition

cards.front: possessive pronoun — what does it mean?
cards.back: A pronoun indicating belonging, such as mine or theirs

cards.front: intensive pronoun — what does it mean?
cards.back: A pronoun form such as herself used to add removable emphasis

cards.front: Apply it: Pronoun case, clarity, and emphasis
cards.back: Identify the pronoun’s job and reference, choose the matching form, and resolve ambiguity without changing the intended meaning.

cards.front: nonrestrictive element — what does it mean?
cards.back: Added information not needed to identify the person or thing

cards.front: restrictive element — what does it mean?
cards.back: Information needed to identify which person or thing is meant

cards.front: parenthetical element — what does it mean?
cards.back: An aside or interruption within a sentence

cards.front: homophone — what does it mean?
cards.back: A word pronounced like another word but differing in meaning or spelling

cards.front: Apply it: Punctuation, spelling, and consistency
cards.back: Identify the intended meaning, distinguish identifying from added information, and choose punctuation and word forms accordingly.

cards.front: register — what does it mean?
cards.back: The kind and level of language suited to a situation and audience

cards.front: tone — what does it mean?
cards.back: The attitude conveyed through wording and presentation

cards.front: precision — what does it mean?
cards.back: Exactness in expressing an intended meaning

cards.front: redundancy — what does it mean?
cards.back: Unnecessary repetition that adds no useful meaning

cards.front: Apply it: Style, register, and precise language
cards.back: Identify audience and purpose, name the exact meaning, and choose wording whose tone and level fit the situation.

cards.front: discussion norm — what does it mean?
cards.back: An agreed expectation that supports a shared conversation

cards.front: active listening — what does it mean?
cards.back: Attending to another person’s meaning and responding to it
